# Catalyst Documentation

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/

## Install the panel

On a fresh Linux host, run this from a root shell. The installer installs Docker
when needed, writes a configured `.env` with generated secrets, and leaves the
stack ready to start:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sudo bash
```

Then [bring the stack up and finish setup](/admin/installation/). Check
[system requirements](/admin/requirements/) first, and add a
[node](/admin/nodes/installing/) before you create game servers. To pin a
release, replace `latest` in the URL with a release tag; the installer can also
[verify its own checksum](/admin/installation/).

## Start here

**Getting started**

New to Catalyst? [What is Catalyst?](/getting-started/what-is-catalyst/)
explains the panel, node, and server, and the
[terminology guide](/getting-started/terminology/) fixes the vocabulary.
Then [create your first game server](/getting-started/first-server/) in minutes.

**Game server guide**

Console, power controls, files, SFTP, backups, databases, tasks, networking,
and sharing your server with others. [Open the guide](/users/overview/).

**Administrator guide**

Install the panel, register nodes, configure networking and storage, manage
users and roles, and keep everything updated. [Open the guide](/admin/overview/).

**API & developers**

Authenticate, call endpoints, handle errors and pagination, and subscribe to
realtime events. [Open the API docs](/api/overview/).

## Catalyst ecosystem

Browse game recipes, panel extensions, and release history on the main site:

**Templates**

Installable recipes for Minecraft, SteamCMD, and community servers in the
[Catalyst Template Catalogue](https://catalystctl.com/templates/).

**Plugins**

Discover and install panel plugins from the
[Catalyst Plugin Marketplace](https://catalystctl.com/plugins/).

**Release notes**

Review new features, bug fixes, and upgrade notes in the
[Catalyst Changelog](https://catalystctl.com/changelog/).

**Catalyst website**

Learn more about Catalyst, architecture, and deployment options on the
[Catalyst Website](https://catalystctl.com/).

## Something broken?

Head straight to [troubleshooting](/troubleshooting/overview/) for server, node,
panel, and networking issues, or look up a specific message in
[common errors](/troubleshooting/common-errors/).

# What is Catalyst?

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/getting-started/what-is-catalyst/
Audience: user, admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Catalyst is a self-hosted game-server control panel. You install it on your own
infrastructure and use it to create, run, and share game servers — Minecraft and
anything else a template supports — through a web interface instead of SSH and
hand-edited config files.

Four ideas explain almost everything in these docs.

## Panel

The **panel** is the web application you log in to. It stores users, roles,
servers, and settings, and it coordinates everything else. Administrators install
and update the panel; server owners mostly live inside it.

## Node

A **node** is a machine that actually runs game servers. Each node runs the
Catalyst **agent**, a small service that starts and stops game servers, streams
console output, and reports health back to the panel. One panel can manage many
nodes, and nodes can live in different datacenters.

## Server

A **server** is one running game — a single Minecraft world with its own files,
memory limit, network ports, backups, and databases. A server always lives on
exactly one node. Server owners manage it through tabs such as **Console**,
**Files**, **Backups**, and **Databases**.

## Allocations

Every server listens on one or more **allocations** — IP address and port pairs
drawn from its node's pool. The primary allocation is the address players join;
[Networking](/users/networking/) explains the rest, and
[connecting to your server](/getting-started/connecting/) shows how to find your
address.

## Templates

A **template** is an installable game recipe: the image, startup command, default
settings, and install script. Administrators manage templates; creating a server
is mostly picking a template and choosing resources.

## Related

- Server owners: [create your first server](/getting-started/first-server/).
- New operators: [install Catalyst](/admin/installation/).
- Integrators: [tour the API](/api/overview/).

---

# Terminology

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/getting-started/terminology/
Audience: user, admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Catalyst reuses a few words with precise meanings. In these docs they always
mean the following:

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Panel** | The Catalyst web application and API you log in to. |
| **Node** | A machine running the Catalyst agent that hosts game servers. |
| **Agent** | The service on a node that runs game servers and talks to the panel. |
| **Server** | One game running on a node, with its own files, limits, ports, and backups. |
| **Template** | A reusable recipe for a game (image, startup command, install script). |
| **Nest** | A category that groups related templates (for example, Minecraft). |
| **Allocation** | An IP + port pair on a node assigned to a server — see [Networking](/users/networking/). |
| **Subuser** | An extra account given limited access to someone else's server. |
| **Task** | A scheduled action on a server, such as a restart or backup (see [Tasks](/users/tasks/)). |
| **Backup** | A restorable snapshot of a server's files. |
| **Database** | A managed database attached to a server (for plugins and mods). |
| **Role** | A named set of permissions administrators assign to users. |
| **API key** | A token that lets scripts and integrations call the Catalyst API. |

A **node** is a machine; a **server** is a game running on that machine. If your
game lags, the problem may be the server's limits or the node's load —
[troubleshooting](/troubleshooting/overview/) helps you tell the difference.

---

# Your First Server

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/getting-started/first-server/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

This guide creates a working Minecraft (Paper) server. The same steps apply to
any game: pick a template, choose resources and an allocation, create, install,
start.

## Prerequisites

- An account on a Catalyst panel (your host or administrator provides this).
- Permission to create servers. If the **New server** button is missing, ask your
  administrator for `server.create` or access to a node.
- A node with free memory, disk, and at least one free allocation. If creation
  fails, ask your administrator — see [server issues](/troubleshooting/server/).

## 1. Create the server

1. Open **Servers** and select **New server**. The **Create new server** dialog
   has five numbered sections — **Details**, **Node**, **Resource Allocation**,
   **Network**, **Startup** — and a summary panel that mirrors the server about to
   be created.
2. **Details:** enter a **Server Name** you will recognize, for example
   `Survival SMP`. **Description** is optional. **Server Owner** appears only if
   you hold `user.create`, `admin.write`, or `*`, and assigning someone else needs
   `user.create` — leave it blank to own the server yourself. Choose the
   **Template**: for Minecraft: Java Edition pick **Minecraft Server
   (Universal)**. Its **SERVER_TYPE** variable picks the server software and
   defaults to Paper. If the template offers an **Image Variant**, leave it on
   **Use default image** unless you need a specific Java runtime.
3. **Node:** choose the **Node** to run it on (usually there is only one). The
   location comes from the node.
4. **Resource Allocation:** **Memory (MB)** and **Disk (MB)** are prefilled from
   the template and **CPU Cores** defaults to `1`; accept them unless you know you
   need more. **Swap (MB)**, **Backup (MB)**, and **Database Allocation** can stay
   blank to use the provider defaults.
5. **Network:** leave **Network Mode** on **Host (port mapping)**. Under **Primary
   Allocation**, pick an **Allocation** (IP + port) for players to join through;
   **Primary Port** fills in from that allocation automatically. (Choose
   **Macvlan** only if your administrator told you to.)
6. **Startup:** these are the template's **Environment Variables**; the defaults
   are a good starting point, and anything marked with a red `*` is required. For
   the Minecraft template, leave **SERVER_TYPE** on `paper` and tick **EULA** to
   accept the Minecraft licence up front (otherwise Catalyst asks after install).
7. If something is missing or out of range, the dialog lists the reason at the
   bottom and **Create server** stays disabled.
8. Select **Create server**. Catalyst creates the server and starts the install
   automatically, then opens its **Console**. Installation can take a few
   minutes — watch the output in the **Console** tab.

**Caution**
Creating a server allocates real resources on the node. Delete test servers you
no longer need so they stop consuming memory and disk.

## 2. Accept the Minecraft EULA

Minecraft servers refuse to run until the EULA is accepted. If you did not tick
**EULA** during creation, Catalyst asks for it in the panel, so you do not edit
any files:

1. When installation finishes, or when you select **Start** in the server
   header, the **Minecraft EULA** dialog appears and the server waits.
2. Scroll to the bottom of the licence — **I Agree** enables once you reach the
   end (or immediately if the text fits without scrolling).
3. Select **I Agree**. Catalyst writes the acceptance for you and starts the
   server. **Decline** leaves the server stopped with status **Error**; starting
   it again asks for the EULA.

## 3. Join the server

1. If the server is not already running, select **Start** in the header and wait
   for the console to print the `Done!` line.
2. Click the address shown in the server header (for example
   `203.0.113.10:25565`) to copy it. See
   [Find your address](/getting-started/connecting/) if it is not visible.
3. In Minecraft, use **Multiplayer → Add Server** and paste the address.

## Related

- [Use the console](/users/console/) — commands, power controls, and logs.
- [Upload files and use SFTP](/users/files/) — worlds, plugins, and configs.
- [Make a backup](/users/backups/) before experimenting.
- [Add a friend](/users/subusers/) as a subuser instead of sharing your login.

---

# Connecting to Your Server

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/getting-started/connecting/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Your game client connects directly to the node running your server — the panel is
for management, not for play.

## Prerequisites

- A server you can access.
- The game client installed on the machine you play from.

## Find your address

1. Open your server. The header shows the address next to the server name as
   `IP:port`, for example `203.0.113.10:25565`.
2. Click the address to copy it — the panel confirms with a **Copied address**
   message.
3. If it shows `n/a`, the panel has no host address for the server's node. Ask
   your administrator to set one before players can join.
4. Extra ports (query, RCON, voice, Bedrock) are listed under **Admin → Ports**.
   The tab opens for `server.delete` (owners) or `admin.write`; changing
   allocations needs `server.network`, which a subuser may not have.

Some hosts put a reverse proxy or custom hostname in front of game ports. If your
host gave you a hostname such as `play.example.com`, use that instead of the raw
IP.

## Connect from the game

- **Minecraft (Java):** Multiplayer → Add Server → paste the address.
- **Minecraft (Bedrock):** Play → Servers → Add Server (check the port — Bedrock
  defaults differ from Java).
- **Other games:** use the address with the game's normal server browser or
  `connect` command.

## If you cannot connect

1. Confirm the status in the header reads **Running**.
2. Confirm you are using the right IP **and** port.
3. Check the console for errors during startup — a crashed server accepts no
   connections.
4. See [server issues](/troubleshooting/server/) and
   [networking issues](/troubleshooting/networking/).

## Related

- [Networking](/users/networking/) — allocations and how players reach your server
- [Console](/users/console/) — watch startup errors that block connections
- [Power controls](/users/power/) — start the server if it is stopped

---

# Overview

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/overview/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Open a server from the **Servers** page and you land on its tab bar. The tabs
you see depend on your permissions on that server and on the server's template.
If a tab is missing, you do not have access to it — or the template does not
support it — rather than something being broken.

| Tab | What it is for | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Console** | Live output and commands. | [Console](/users/console/) |
| **Files** | Browse, edit, upload, download, archive. | [Files](/users/files/) |
| **SFTP** | Connect with FileZilla or WinSCP for big transfers. | [SFTP](/users/sftp/) |
| **Backups** | Create, restore, download, pin, and prune snapshots. | [Backups](/users/backups/) |
| **Tasks** | Scheduled restarts, backups, and commands. | [Tasks](/users/tasks/) |
| **Databases** | Databases for plugins and mods. | [Databases](/users/databases/) |
| **Metrics** | CPU, memory, disk, and network graphs. | [Metrics & Alerts](/users/metrics/) |
| **Alerts** | Notifications when a metric crosses a threshold. | [Metrics & Alerts](/users/metrics/) |
| **Activity** | Who did what, and when. | [Activity](/users/activity/) |
| **Mod Manager** | Mods, datapacks, and modpacks from Modrinth or CurseForge. | [Mods & Plugins](/users/mods-plugins/) |
| **Plugin Manager** | Plugins from Modrinth or CurseForge. | [Mods & Plugins](/users/mods-plugins/) |
| **Configuration** | Startup command, variables, and config files. | [Startup & Variables](/users/startup/) |
| **Users** | Give friends limited access. | [Users & Subusers](/users/subusers/) |
| **Settings** | Server name, maintenance, reinstall, clone. | [Reinstalling](/users/reinstalling/) |
| **Admin** | Allocations, image, resources, owner transfer, danger zone. | [Networking](/users/networking/) |

Power controls — **Start**, **Stop**, **Restart**, and **Kill** — sit in the
server header, above the tabs. See [Power controls](/users/power/).

## Related

- [Networking](/users/networking/) — how players reach your server through its
  allocations.
- [Cloning](/users/cloning/) — copy a server's settings, or its whole world.

**Note**
Tab labels on this page are the English names. Your panel may be translated,
and a plugin can add its own tabs next to the built-in ones.

---

# Console

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/console/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-16

The **Console** tab shows everything your game server prints — startup messages,
player joins, errors — as it happens. It keeps up to 2,000 lines in its buffer;
older output scrolls away.

## Prerequisites

- A server you can access, with the `console.read` permission to watch output
  and `console.write` to send commands.
- A running server to send commands — the command box is disabled otherwise.

The status pill at the top left tells you where the live stream stands:
**Live**, **Connecting**, **Reconnecting**, or **Disconnected**.

## Run a command

1. Type into the command box at the bottom (`$`) and press Enter, or select
   **Send**.
2. Commands run as the server itself, exactly as if you typed them into its own
   terminal:
   - Minecraft: `say Hello`, `whitelist add Notch`, `tps`
   - Source games: `status`, `changelevel de_dust2`

The box is disabled unless the server is running, the stream is connected, and
you have the `console.write` permission. Press the **Up** and **Down** arrows to
step through recent commands, or **Tab** to complete from history.

**Caution**
Console commands bypass most safety rails. A wrong command can ban players or
delete data. When in doubt, [make a backup](/users/backups/) first.

## Console controls

The toolbar above the output has one control per stream plus a few view tools:

- **stdout / stderr / system / stdin** — toggle which streams are shown. On a
  narrow screen they collapse into a **Streams** menu with the active count.
- **Find** (the magnifier, or **Ctrl+F** while the console has focus) — search
  the visible output; Enter jumps to the next match, Shift+Enter to the previous
  one.
- **Buffer size** — how many lines the terminal keeps in view: `500`, `1K`, or
  `2K` (1K by default).
- **Follow** — auto-scroll as new output arrives. Scrolling up turns it off and
  shows a **Follow** button to resume.
- **Copy output** and **Download output** — copy the visible lines, or save them
  as a `.log` file.
- **Clear console** — clears the view (it does not delete stored logs).
- **Expand** — full-screen the console; **Esc** or **Collapse** returns.

## Read a crash

When a server will not stay up:

1. Press **Start** and watch the first 50 lines — the real error is usually
   near the top, not at the end.
2. Use **Find** to jump to `ERROR`, `Exception`, `missing`, or `port already in
   use`.
3. Common causes and fixes live in [server issues](/troubleshooting/server/).

## Console vs. logs

The console is a live view, not permanent storage. For history, use the
**Activity** tab (who did what), **Download output** for the current buffer, or
download log files from the **Files** tab (usually under `logs/`). Realtime
integrations should use the [event streams API](/api/websockets/) rather than
scraping the console.

## Related

- [Power controls](/users/power/)
- [Tasks](/users/tasks/) — run commands automatically

---

# Power Controls

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/power/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Power controls sit in the server header on the server page, and on the card or
row for each server on the **Servers** page.

## Prerequisites

- A server you own or can access. The controls are hidden without the matching
  permission (see below).
- An online node — power actions fail while the node's agent is offline.

| Action | What it does | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Start** | Boots the server. | After creating, editing configs, or a crash. |
| **Restart** | Stops gracefully, then starts, using your saved startup command. | After config or plugin changes. |
| **Stop** | Asks the game to shut down cleanly. | Before editing world files or upgrading. |
| **Kill** | Force-stops the server immediately. | Only when Stop/Restart hang (the world may not save). |

Each button is enabled only when it makes sense for the current state — for
example, **Start** is disabled while the server is already running. You also
need the matching permission: **Start** needs `server.start`, **Stop** needs
`server.stop`, **Kill** needs `server.kill`, and **Restart** needs **both**
`server.start` and `server.stop`. Without them the controls are hidden.

Pressing **Kill** always asks for confirmation first: *"This will
force-terminate the server process immediately without saving. Data may be
lost. Are you sure?"*

While a server is installing, the header offers **Cancel install** (needs
`server.install` or `server.reinstall`). It kills the stuck installer and resets
the server to stopped; partial install files are kept. You can then reinstall or
start normally.

## The safe order

1. Warn players if anyone is online.
2. Prefer **Restart** over **Kill** — graceful stops let the game save the world.
3. After changing configs, plugins, or startup variables, always restart; most
   games only read those files at boot.

## If a server will not stop

1. Wait 60 seconds — large worlds take a while to save.
2. Use **Kill** as a last resort.
3. If it still shows as running, check [server issues](/troubleshooting/server/)
   or ask your administrator — the node agent may need attention.

## If a server will not start

If the node denies host networking for the server, **Start** answers with a
dialog titled *"Host networking is disabled on this node"*. Selecting **Enable
and start** turns host networking on for the node (you need the
`node.agent_control` permission), then starts the server.

## Automate it

Nightly restarts and similar routines belong in [Tasks](/users/tasks/), not in
manual clicking.

## Related

- [Console](/users/console/) — watch the boot log after starting
- [Tasks](/users/tasks/) — scheduled power actions

---

# Files

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/files/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

The **Files** tab is a file manager for your server: configs, worlds, plugins,
and logs. It is the right tool for small, targeted changes. For large transfers
(whole world folders, modpacks), use [SFTP](/users/sftp/) instead.

## Prerequisites

- A server you can access, with the `file.read` permission to browse and
  `file.write` to change anything.
- For uploads, a file size within the upload limit your administrator set.

The left rail is the **Directory Tree**; the breadcrumb and filter box above the
list move around the current folder.

## Everyday tasks

- **Open or edit a file:** click a file (or **Open File** in its menu). Config
  files open in the built-in editor with syntax highlighting. Select **Save**
  (or **Ctrl+S**), then [restart](/users/power/) the server so the game re-reads
  the file. **Revert** undoes your changes; closing with unsaved edits asks
  first.
- **Upload:** select **Upload**, then **Choose Files** in the upload panel, or
  drop files straight onto the file list. Files larger than the upload limit
  your administrator set are rejected with the limit shown.
- **Download:** open a file's menu (the **⋯** button or right-click) and choose
  **Download**. Directories cannot be downloaded as a batch in the browser —
  use [SFTP](/users/sftp/) to pull a whole folder.
- **Create:** select **New File** or **New Folder**.
- **Rename:** choose **Rename** from a file's menu and type the new name.
- **Copy a path:** choose **Copy Path** to put the full server path on your
  clipboard — handy when pasting into a command or a support thread.
- **Permissions:** choose **Permissions** to set the octal mode (for example
  `644` for files, `755` for folders).
- **Delete:** select one or more entries and choose **Delete**, then confirm.
- **Compress / Extract:** select entries and choose **Compress**, or open a
  `.zip` / `.tar.gz` to preview its contents read-only and **Extract** it to a
  target path.
- **Find an error:** game logs usually live under `logs/` — open the latest log
  after a crash before asking for help.

**Caution**
Delete, rename, and extract all act immediately once confirmed. There is no
undo in the file manager — [a backup](/users/backups/) is the undo.

## Rules that prevent data loss

1. **Stop the server** before replacing world files or large data directories.
   Editing live world data while the game holds it in memory corrupts saves.
2. **Back up before big changes.** [One backup](/users/backups/) takes seconds
   and undoes almost any mistake.
3. The file manager cannot see outside your server directory — that is
   intentional isolation, not a bug.

## Common locations

| Game | Where things live |
| --- | --- |
| Minecraft | `server.properties`, `config/`, `plugins/`, `world/`, `logs/` |
| Source/CS2 | `cfg/`, `addons/`, `maps/` |
| Generic | Check your template's documentation or ask your host. |

Exact paths depend on the template. If a path listed here does not exist on your
server, read the template description or ask your administrator rather than
creating it by hand.

## Related

- [SFTP](/users/sftp/) — large transfers and whole folders
- [Backups](/users/backups/) — the undo button for file changes
- [Startup & Variables](/users/startup/) — template-declared config files

---

# SFTP

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/sftp/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

SFTP gives you a fast, resumable connection for big transfers — uploading a
modpack, downloading a world, syncing with an external editor. For small edits,
the editor in the [Files tab](/users/files/) is faster.

## Prerequisites

- A server you can access, with `file.read` — the **SFTP** tab appears with the
  same access as the **Files** tab, so a write-only subuser never sees it.
- SFTP enabled on the node. If it is off, the tab says so.
- An SFTP client such as FileZilla, WinSCP, or Cyberduck.

## Connect

1. Open the server's **SFTP** tab. It shows **Host**, **Port**, **Username** and
   **Password**, each with a copy button, plus a **Quick Connect URI** you can
   paste into a client that understands `sftp://` URLs.
2. In your client, choose protocol **SFTP** — Catalyst does not offer plain FTP
   — and paste the host, port, username and password exactly as shown.
3. You land in your server's root directory, the same files as the **Files**
   tab. Uploads, deletes, renames and permission changes show up there as they
   happen.

Two details:

- The **username is the server's ID**, and the host and port belong to the
  **node** that runs the server.
- The **password is a temporary token, not your panel password.** The tab shows
  how long is left. Pick a **Token lifetime** and select **Rotate password** —
  or **Generate new** once it has expired — to issue a fresh one.

Every user gets their own credentials. If you are the owner, **Active SFTP
Sessions** lists each user's session with its expiry and a revoke button, plus
**Revoke all sessions**. Removing a user from the server revokes their SFTP
sessions immediately.

If the tab says *"SFTP is disabled on this server."*, SFTP is turned off for the
node — ask your administrator to enable it.

## Good practice

- **Stop the server** before uploading or replacing world data or databases.
- If your client warns about an unknown host key on first connect, verify the
  fingerprint with your administrator before accepting it.

## Troubleshooting

- **Authentication failed:** credentials rotate — copy them fresh from the SFTP
  tab instead of reusing a saved password.
- **Connection refused or timed out:** the node may block the SFTP port, or your
  network may block outbound SSH. See
  [networking issues](/troubleshooting/networking/).
- **Transfers stall on huge folders:** archive them first, upload one file, then
  extract it in the **Files** tab.

## Related

- [Files](/users/files/) — browse, edit, and extract without a client
- [Backups](/users/backups/) — download a full snapshot instead of copying files

---

# Backups

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/backups/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

A backup is a restorable snapshot of your server's files. Make one before every
risky change — updates, new plugins, world edits, reinstalls.

## Prerequisites

- `backup.read` to see the list, `backup.create` to make a backup,
  `backup.restore` to restore one, `backup.delete` to delete one, and
  `backup.download` to download one.
- For a restore, the server must be stopped.

## Create a backup

1. Open **Backups** and select **Create backup** (the same button appears when
   the list is empty).
2. Optionally give it a name, for example `before-1.21-update`. Leave it blank
   and the panel generates one from the current timestamp.
3. Leave **Compress backup (gzip)** checked unless you need a plain archive.
   Unchecking it writes an uncompressed `.tar`, which is faster to create and
   restore but larger on disk and slower to transfer.
4. If your administrator enabled a secondary backup drive, **Copy to the
   secondary drive** appears. Tick it to keep a second copy on that drive as
   well; the row shows a **Secondary drive** badge once the copy lands. The
   option only applies to **Local** and **Stream** storage.
5. Select **Create backup** and wait for the status to reach **Completed**
   before stopping the server or changing files.

## Restore a backup

1. **Stop the server first** — **Restore** stays disabled until it is stopped.
2. Find the snapshot and select **Restore**.
3. Confirm the dialog. It names the backup and warns that the server must be
   stopped and that current files will be overwritten.
4. Wait for the restore to finish, then start the server and check the world
   loads before deleting the backup you restored from.

The restore runs on the node: the archive is extracted into a staging
directory and only swapped over the live files once the whole tree has been
validated. Symbolic links are restored as they were. If the restore is refused —
an unreadable archive, not enough free space, or a link pointing outside the
server directory — the server returns to **Stopped**, the panel reports the
reason, and your current files are left untouched.

**Caution**
Restore overwrites the server's current files. When in doubt, back up the
*current* files first, so you can go back either way.

## Download and delete

- **Download** saves the snapshot as a `.tar.gz`, or a `.tar` for an
  uncompressed backup. Keep critical backups off-site: a backup on the same node
  does not survive node loss. When the node is offline and the backup has a
  secondary-drive copy, the download is served from that copy instead.
- **Delete** removes a snapshot. The confirmation names the backup and warns
  that the action cannot be undone.

## Pin a backup

Pinned backups are exempt from the retention rules below and do not count
towards **Keep last N**. Pinning needs the `backup.pin` permission — owning the
server does not grant it, because exempting a backup from the retention limit is
an administrator decision. Panel administrators hold it through `admin.write`.

- **Pin** on a backup's row adds a **Pinned** badge; **Unpin** makes it subject
  to the retention rules again.
- **Ignore limit** in the create dialog pins a backup from the start.

Pinned backups still use the server's storage allocation, and pinning does not
copy them off the node — download anything you must keep permanently.

## Backup settings

The **Backup settings** card controls where backups go and how long they are
kept. Changing it needs `backup.create`; changing the storage mode or the S3 /
SFTP credentials additionally needs admin or node-manage access.

- **Storage mode** — **Local** and **Stream (backend-local)** use the backup
  space allocated to the server. **S3** and **SFTP** store backups on
  infrastructure you provide and work without a local allocation.
- **Keep last N** — keep at most N backups (0 = unlimited, up to 1000).
- **Max age (days)** — delete backups older than N days (0 = unlimited, up to
  3650).
- **Save settings** applies the change.

A background job enforces these rules about every six hours.

When the server has no provider allocation, the tab warns: *"Provider backup
allocation is not available for this server. Local and Stream storage modes
require an allocation. Configure your own S3 or SFTP storage to enable
backups."* Configure S3 or SFTP above, or ask your administrator for an
allocation.

## Good habits

- Back up before changes, plus a recurring [task](/users/tasks/) for daily or
  weekly safety nets.
- Download critical backups off-site. Node-level disaster recovery is an
  administrator concern ([admin backups](/admin/backups/)).

## Related

- [Tasks](/users/tasks/) — automate backups
- [Reinstalling](/users/reinstalling/) — backup first, always

---

# Databases

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/databases/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Many plugins (permissions, economy, logging, Dynmap) need a database. The
**Databases** tab provisions one for your server without you touching a
database server.

## Prerequisites

- `database.read` to see the tab, `database.create` to add a database,
  `database.rotate` to rotate a password, `database.delete` to remove one.
- A database allocation on the server **and** at least one database host
  configured by your administrator. Without either, the tab is not shown at all.

## Create a database

1. Open **Databases**. The header shows how many you have used, for example
   *2 / 3 databases used*.
2. Choose a host from the **Select host** dropdown — each option is listed as
   `name (host:port)`.
3. Type a database name (for example `dynmap`) and select **Create**.
   - The name must start with a letter and use only lowercase letters, numbers
     and underscores, up to 32 characters.
   - Leave it blank or shorter than three characters and the panel generates a
     safe name for you.
4. The **Database credentials** dialog opens. Copy the **Host** (shown as
   `host:port`), **Database**, **Username** and **Password**.
5. Paste them into the plugin's config file through [Files](/users/files/), then
   restart the server.

**Create** is disabled once you reach the allocation limit. Deleting the server
also removes its database records.

**Caution**
The dialog warns that the password *"is shown only once and cannot be displayed
again."* Copy it before selecting **Done** — if you lose it, rotate it.

## Rotate credentials

1. Select **Rotate** on the database.
2. The **Database credentials** dialog opens with a fresh password. Copy it
   immediately — it is shown once.
3. Update every plugin config that uses it, then restart the server and check
   the logs for successful connections.

## Delete a database

Select **Delete** and confirm. The dialog warns that this permanently drops the
database and its credentials.

## Troubleshooting

- **The tab is missing:** the server has no database allocation, or no database
  host is available to you — ask your administrator for one.
- **Plugin cannot connect:** use the host and port from the credentials dialog,
  not `localhost` — the database usually runs on shared infrastructure. Then
  confirm the username and password and that the server was restarted after the
  config change.
- **Access denied after rotation:** one of your configs still has the old
  password.
- **Limit reached:** delete a database you no longer need, or ask your
  administrator to raise the per-server allocation.

## Related

- [Storage](/admin/storage/) — where administrators configure database hosts
- [Files](/users/files/) — edit the plugin config that uses the database
- [Startup & Variables](/users/startup/) — variables some plugins need

---

# Startup & Variables

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/startup/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-16

The **Configuration** tab controls how your server boots: the startup command,
the variables the template exposes (game version, memory, extra flags), and a
form editor for the server's config files.

## Prerequisites

- A server you can access, with the `server.update` permission to change the
  startup command, variables, and template config files.
- A [restart](/users/power/) after the change — most games read these values
  only at boot.

## Change a startup variable

1. Open your server's **Configuration** tab and find the **Startup variables**
   section.
2. Edit the value. Variables render as a text box, a number box, or a toggle
   depending on their type; required variables are marked with `*`.
3. Select **Save**. A **Reset** button appears while you have unsaved changes
   and discards them.
4. [Restart](/users/power/) the server — startup variables only take effect at
   boot.

Values are validated as you type: a bad number, a missing required value, an
out-of-range value, or a value outside the allowed list is flagged under the
field, and the save is rejected with the offending fields marked.

## Change the startup command

1. In **Configuration**, edit the **Startup command** field. Templates use
   placeholders such as `{{MEMORY}}` and `{{PORT}}` that the panel fills in at
   boot.
2. Select **Save**.
3. Select **Reset to default** to restore the template's original command. When
   your command differs from the template, the template default is shown below
   the field as a clickable link that restores it.

## Edit config files

The **Config files** section loads the files the template declares (for example
`server.properties`) and lets you edit them in a **Form** or **Raw** view, with a
search box to jump to a key. Select **Save config** to write the file. Files not
declared by the template are edited through [Files](/users/files/) instead.

## Rules

- Only change what you understand. A bad startup flag or config value is the
  most common self-inflicted reason a server enters a boot loop.
- Memory variables must stay within the server's allocated limits — the game
  cannot use more than the server owns.
- If the server worked before your change and boot-loops now, revert the last
  edit first and ask questions later.

## Templates define what is editable

Which variables exist, their defaults, and their allowed values come from the
server's **template** (set by your administrator). If a template exposes no
startup variables, the section stays empty. If you need a variable the template
does not expose, ask your administrator.

## Related

- [Reinstalling](/users/reinstalling/) — when a fresh install is cleaner than debugging
- [Server issues](/troubleshooting/server/) — boot loops and crashes

---

# CPU Pinning

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/cpu-pinning/
Audience: user, admin
Last verified: 2026-11-20

CPU pinning restricts a server to a numbered subset of its node's CPUs. Use it
when a game is picky about core locality, when you want two heavy servers on
clearly separate cores, or when a node mixes fast and slow cores and you want a
server on the fast ones.

**Note — What pinning does not do**
Pinning does not reserve a CPU. The server's **CPU allocation** still caps how
much CPU time it may use, and other servers may be pinned to the same CPUs —
they then share that time by weight. To place a server and cap it, set both.

## Prerequisites

- A server you can manage, with the `server.resources` permission (owners and
  administrators always have it).
- The node's agent must have reported its CPU set. Nodes that have never
  connected, or that run an older agent, show a text field instead of a picker
  and the pin is only checked when the server starts.

## Pin a server

1. Open the server and choose **Edit resources** (the pencil next to the
   resource summary).
2. Under **CPU pinning**, pick the CPUs. **All CPUs** clears the pin; the
   canonical form of your selection is shown next to the label.
3. Save, then **restart** the server: a pin applies when the server starts, so
   changing it on a running server takes effect at its next start.

For a new server, the same field is in the **Resources** step of the create
dialog.

## Rules

- A pin must name at least as many CPUs as the server's **CPU allocation**. A
  2-core server pinned to one CPU can never spend its allocation, so the panel
  refuses the save and tells you which value to change.
- A pin may name more CPUs than the allocation. That is the normal way to let a
  2-core server spread across four CPUs.
- Only CPUs the node has are accepted. The picker offers exactly the node's
  reported set; the server refuses anything else with the available set named.
- A pin is a property of the node's CPU numbering, not of the server. Moving a
  server to another node is covered below.

## Moving a server

- **Cloning** to the same node keeps the pin. Cloning to another node keeps it
  only when that node has the same CPUs; otherwise the review step warns that
  the clone will not be pinned, and you must acknowledge it before cloning.
- **Transferring** a pinned server to another node is refused while the pin
  cannot be satisfied there. Clear the pin, transfer, then pin again.

## Troubleshooting

| Message | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| The pinned CPUs are not available on this node | The node's CPU set changed since the pin was saved (a CPU was taken offline, or the server was moved) | Edit resources and pick CPUs the node has, or clear the pin |
| CPU pinning covers *n* CPUs but the server is allocated *m* cores | The pin is narrower than the allocation | Pin more CPUs, or lower the CPU allocation in the same save |
| The pin is only checked when the server starts | The node has not reported a CPU set yet | Start the server; the node refuses an impossible pin with the same message |

## Related

- [Metrics & Alerts](/users/metrics/) — CPU usage is reported per core
- [Cloning](/users/cloning/) — how node-specific settings move between nodes
- [Startup & Variables](/users/startup/) — changing the command a pinned server runs

---

# Reinstalling

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/reinstalling/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Reinstalling replaces your server files with a fresh copy from its template. Use
it when an installation is damaged beyond easy repair — corrupted jars, mangled
configs after a bad edit, or a version jump you would rather do cleanly.

## Prerequisites

1. [Create a backup](/users/backups/) and wait for it to finish.
2. Download anything the backup might not cover that you care about (or verify
   the backup completed — do not skip this).
3. Tell your players: the server will be offline and the world may reset.

You need the `server.reinstall` permission (the server owner has it by default).

## Reinstall

1. Stop the server. **Reinstall** stays disabled while the server is running.
2. Open the server's **Settings** tab and find the **Maintenance** row.
3. Select **Reinstall**.
4. Confirm the **Reinstall server?** dialog — it warns that every file in the
   server directory is deleted. Select **Reinstall** to proceed.
5. Watch the install output in the [console](/users/console/) until it finishes.
6. Start the server again with [power controls](/users/power/). A Minecraft
   server shows a **Minecraft EULA** dialog on the next start — scroll to the
   bottom and select **I Agree** to let it boot, or **Decline** to stop it.
7. Re-apply anything the template install does not restore (configs, plugins,
   and so on).

## If an install gets stuck

A server stuck in the **installing** state shows a **Cancel install** button
next to **Reinstall**. It kills the stuck installer and resets the server to
stopped so you can try again; partial install files are kept.

**Caution**
Reinstalling deletes current files. It is not an upgrade path for worlds you
want to keep unless you restore them afterwards from the backup.

## Alternatives to consider first

- One broken config? Revert that file instead of wiping everything.
- Boot loop after a variable change? Revert the variable ([startup](/users/startup/)).
- Install script out of date but files fine? The **Admin** tab's **Container**
  section has **Rebuild** (needs `server.rebuild`): it re-runs the install
  command and keeps existing files instead of deleting them. Administrators
  reinstall from the same section.
- Just want a second server with the same setup? [Clone it](/users/cloning/)
  instead of starting from scratch — a configuration clone installs fresh, a
  full clone copies the world too.

## Related

- [Backups](/users/backups/) — restore what a reinstall wiped
- [Startup & Variables](/users/startup/) — re-apply template variables
- [Cloning](/users/cloning/) — duplicate instead of rebuilding

---

# Cloning

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/cloning/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Cloning creates a new server from an existing one: a second deployment of the
same setup, or a duplicate of a configured world.

## Prerequisites

- The `server.clone` permission (legacy `server.create` grants still work) and
  access to the source server.
- To clone onto another node, `server.transfer` and access to that node.
- For a full clone, the source server stopped — the dialog offers **Stop source
  and continue** if it is running.

## Choose a clone mode

Both modes copy the panel configuration: template, variables, startup command,
resource limits, network mode, backup policy and restart policy. They differ in
what happens to the files.

| | Full clone | Configuration clone |
|---|---|---|
| Panel configuration | Copied | Copied |
| Server files (world, plugins, configs) | Copied | Not copied |
| Install after cloning | No — files are already there | Yes — the template installer runs |
| Source server must be stopped | Yes | No |

Use a **full clone** to duplicate a live world or a hand-configured modpack. Use
a **configuration clone** for another server with the same settings but a clean
installation.

## Clone a server

1. Open the server, then **Settings**, and find the **Maintenance** row.
2. Select **Clone**.
3. Choose the mode — the dialog starts on **Configuration clone**.
4. Give the new server a name (it defaults to the source name plus `Copy`).
5. Choose the **node** it will be created on.
6. Choose the **network mode**. For host or bridge networking, optionally pick a
   **Network Allocation**; otherwise leave it on **Auto-assign**.
7. Adjust memory, CPU and disk if the clone should differ. Panel administrators
   can also set the clone's **Server Owner**; otherwise you own it.
8. Tick what else to copy under **Also copy** — **Sub-users**, **Role grants**,
   **Scheduled tasks**, **Databases** and **Installed mods**. Tasks, databases
   and installed-mod records are off by default: two servers running the same
   task can conflict, a copied database is provisioned empty rather than shared,
   and a full clone already copies the mod files.
9. Select **Review changes**, review the change list, tick any warnings, then
   confirm.

**Caution — Full clones require a stopped source**
A full clone reads the source server's files directly. If the source is running,
Catalyst blocks the clone and offers **Stop source and continue**. Stopping the
server disconnects its players.

## Confirm the node-specific changes

Cloning onto a **different node** re-resolves everything tied to the node, and
the panel creates nothing until you have reviewed and accepted those changes:

- **Node** and **location**.
- **IP address** — a fresh IP from the new node's pool, or the allocation you
  chose.
- **Primary port and port mappings** — host ports are reassigned so the clone
  cannot collide with a server already on the node.
- **Data directory** — the new node stores server data under its own path.
- **SFTP endpoint** — the clone is reachable on the target node's hostname and
  port.

If something blocks the clone — the node is offline, it does not support the
network mode, it lacks memory, CPU or free disk space, or no allocation is
free — the panel lists it as a blocker and will not continue until it is
resolved.

The confirmation is bound to the changes you reviewed: if the options change
between the review and the confirmation (for example someone else claims the
allocation you picked), the panel discards the review and asks you to review
again.

## While the clone is created

- A **configuration clone** starts installing immediately. Watch progress in the
  console, exactly like a new server.
- A **full clone** sits in a **Cloning** state while its files are copied and
  cannot be started until the copy finishes. Large servers and cross-node clones
  take longer.

If a file copy fails, the new server is left in place and stopped, with the
reason in its console log. Delete it and run the clone again.

## What is not copied

- **Backup archives** and the backup list — backups belong to the source server.
- **Database contents.** A clone can create a new, empty database when you tick
  **Databases**; it never points at the source database.
- **Logs, metrics and crash history.** Every clone starts with a clean history.
- **Backup storage credentials.** The clone falls back to local backup storage
  instead of inheriting S3 or SFTP credentials.

## After cloning

1. Start the new server and confirm it boots.
2. Check the connection details — the address and port are node-specific, so
   they may differ from the source ([networking](/users/networking/)).
3. If you copied databases, reconnect the application inside the server to its
   new database and credentials.

## Related

- [Networking](/users/networking/) — the clone's address and ports
- [Backups](/users/backups/) — the clone never inherits the source's backups
- [Tasks](/users/tasks/) — tasks are not copied unless you tick them

---

# Mods & Plugins

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/mods-plugins/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

A template that configures a **Mod Manager** or a **Plugin Manager** gives the
server that tab; a template that configures neither has no such tab. Which one
you get depends on the template, not on the game, and a template may configure
both. The **Mod Manager** covers mods, datapacks and modpacks (`mods.manage`);
the **Plugin Manager** covers plugins (`plugins.manage`).

## Prerequisites

- A template with one of the two managers — otherwise the tab is not shown.
- `mods.manage` or `plugins.manage` for installing, updating, and removing.
- A [restart](/users/power/) after every install, update, or removal.

## Provider API keys

The managers search third-party providers. Modrinth and CurseForge each need an
API key, and a provider without one is hidden from the **Provider** list. If
every provider the template offers needs a key that is not configured, the tab
shows **No providers available** — ask an administrator to add it under
**Admin → System → Mod Manager API Keys**.

## Install a mod or datapack

1. Open the **Mod Manager** tab and its **Browse** sub-tab.
2. Type in the search box. Results update as you type; Enter or **Search**
   restarts the search at page 1.
3. Narrow the results with **Provider**, **Mod loader**, **Content type**,
   **Sort by**, **Category**, and the game version box.
4. Pick a result, choose a release in **Select version**, then select
   **Install**.
5. [Restart](/users/power/) the server, then read the
   [console](/users/console/) for load errors.

Filter behaviour:

- **Mod loader** starts on **Any loader**; the options are Forge, NeoForge,
  Fabric and Quilt, and the filter appears only for Minecraft providers.
- **Content type** offers only what the template enables: **Mods**,
  **Datapacks**, **Modpacks**.
- **Sort by** — **Default order**, **Downloads**, **Followers**, **Newest**,
  **Recently updated**, **Relevance**. Default order means relevance while
  searching and downloads while browsing.
- **Category** appears only for Modrinth, the only provider that publishes its
  categories.
- The game version box starts empty and shows **Any version (server: X)** as a
  placeholder — no version filter is applied until you type one. Modrinth
  suggests versions as you type.

The **Installed** sub-tab lists every file the manager tracks, with
**Has Updates**, **Tracked** and **Untracked** filters and name/size/date
sorting.

## Install a modpack

1. Open the **Mod Manager** and select the **Install pack** sub-tab. It only
   exists when the template enables the **Modpacks** content type.
2. Choose **Modpack archive** — `.zip`, `.mrpack`, `.mr`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`,
   `.tgz`, `.tar.xz`, `.txz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tbz2` — or paste a direct `http`
   or `https` link in **Or install from a URL**. The backend also extracts
   `.tar.zst` and `.tzst`, which the file picker does not list.
3. Optionally set **Install into** to a subdirectory. Leave it empty to install
   into the server root, which is what most packs expect.
4. Select **Install modpack**. The install runs on the node, so you can leave
   the tab; the phases are **Extracting archive**, **Downloading mods**,
   **Applying overrides** and **Finishing up**, with a file count at each.
5. [Restart](/users/power/) to load the pack, then read the
   [console](/users/console/) for errors.

The finished panel reports **Pack format**, **Mods downloaded** and **Overrides
applied**, plus **Skipped entries** when anything was left out. Warnings mean an
individual file could not be fetched — the rest of the pack still installs, and
you can add that file by hand later.

For Modrinth and CurseForge packs the manager reads the pack manifest:

- files are downloaded from the provider instead of being re-uploaded;
- client-only files are skipped — `env.server = "unsupported"` entries and
  anything under `client-overrides/` never reach the server;
- the pack's `overrides/` are merged into the install directory, after the
  manifest files, so the author's configs win;
- the manifest and pack scaffolding are removed from the server directory
  afterwards.

**Caution**
A modpack overwrites the configs it ships. Back up first
([backups](/users/backups/)) if the server already has a working setup.

The pack's mods appear in **Installed**, so **Check Updates** covers them.

## Install a plugin

1. Open the **Plugin Manager** tab and its **Browse** sub-tab.
2. Search, optionally filtering by game version (**Any game version**, or
   **Server version (X)** for the detected version) and by provider.
3. Sort with **Trending**, **Popular**, **Top rated**, **Recently updated** or
   **Newest**.
4. Pick the plugin and its **Version**, select **Install**, then restart the
   server.

## Keep mods and plugins up to date

1. Open the manager's **Installed** sub-tab.
2. Select **Check Updates**. Anything with a newer release is flagged, and the
   tab badge and the **Has Updates** filter show the count.
3. Select the items to update, or leave the selection empty to update
   everything that has an update, then select **Update**. The confirmation
   warns that an update can break compatibility — back up first
   ([backups](/users/backups/)).
4. Restart the server.

A mod the panel did not install shows as **untracked**: it has no version
metadata, so you update it by hand through [Files](/users/files/).

## Remove a mod or plugin

In the **Installed** sub-tab, tick the files (or use **Select all**) and select
**Remove**, then confirm. Restart the server. Leftover configs in `config/` or
`plugins/` are harmless but can confuse a replacement.

## Rules for a stable server

1. **Match versions.** A mod built for a different game version is the top
   cause of boot failures. The manager filters versions for you; manual uploads
   through [Files](/users/files/) do not.
2. **Add one at a time**, so a crash has one suspect instead of ten.

## Related

- [Console](/users/console/) — load errors after an install
- [Backups](/users/backups/) — back up before changing mods
- [Files](/users/files/) — edit configs the managers do not cover

---

# Networking

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/networking/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

An **allocation** is an IP address + port pair on your node. Your **primary**
allocation is the address players join through; additional allocations serve
extra ports (query, RCON, voice, Bedrock vs. Java).

## Prerequisites

- A server you can access — the address is shown in its header and on its card.
- To add or remove allocations, the **Admin** tab's **Ports** section, which
  needs the `server.network` permission (panel administrators have it through
  `admin.write`).

## Find your server's address

The address is shown in the server header and on the server card in your list —
`IP:port`, using the primary allocation. See
[connecting to your server](/getting-started/connecting/) for how to read and
share it.

## See and manage allocations

Allocations are managed in the server's **Admin** tab under **Ports**. The node
owns the pool of addresses; if you need another port (for example for a
plugin's web map), ask your administrator.

1. Pick a free address from the **Select allocation** list and set the port it
   maps to inside the server (the field the panel labels **Container port**).
2. Select **Add allocation**.
3. Each row shows the host address (`IP:host port`) mapped to the server-side
   port, marks the **Primary** one with a star, and labels the rest
   **Secondary**.
4. **Set primary** promotes a secondary allocation; **Remove allocation** deletes
   one. Removing an allocation from a running server closes its firewall rule
   immediately and disconnects anyone using that port, so the panel asks you to
   confirm first.

If the node's pool is empty, the section links straight to the node's
allocations page.

## Rules

- Never point two servers at the same allocation — the second one fails to bind
  with `port already in use`. See [server issues](/troubleshooting/server/).
- Changing the network mode or primary port is part of the server's admin
  configuration, not something you change from the game itself.
- If players cannot connect, first confirm you are sharing the primary
  allocation and the server is running.

## Related

- [Connecting to your server](/getting-started/connecting/) — find and share your address
- [Admin networking](/admin/networking/) — how administrators manage node address pools
- [Server issues](/troubleshooting/server/) — when players cannot connect

---

# Users & Subusers

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/subusers/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

The **Users** tab (titled **Users & Access**) adds subusers: extra accounts with
limited access to your server. Your friend signs in with their own account and
sees only what you allow.

## Prerequisites

- A server you own or administer — plain subusers cannot invite others.
- The permissions you intend to grant: you cannot grant a permission you do not
  hold yourself.
- For invites by email, a panel with email delivery configured. Without it, the
  panel shows a copyable invite link instead.

## Invite a subuser

1. Open the server's **Users** tab and find **Invite user**.
2. Enter their panel account email.
3. Pick a preset:
   - **Read-only** — view the server, console, files, databases and alerts.
   - **Power user** — read-only plus power actions, console commands, file
     editing, backups and database management.
   - **Full access** — the full preset: also startup changes, ports, tasks,
     cloning, mods and plugins, transfer, and deleting the server. It does not
     include `backup.pin` ([pinning a backup](/users/backups/#pin-a-backup) is
     reserved for explicit grants).
   - **Custom** — tick exactly the permissions you want; they are grouped by
     area (console, file, server, …).
4. Select **Send invite**.

When email delivery is available the panel emails the invite; otherwise — or if
delivery fails — an **Invite link** dialog appears. Select **Copy** and send the
link yourself. The invite is bound to the email you entered: the invitee accepts
it by signing in with that address, or by creating an account for it on the
invite page. Someone signed in as a different account is asked to sign out
first. Keep the link private — it grants the assigned permissions to whoever
opens it with that account.

Invites expire after 7 days. A pending invite has **Copy link** to share it
again, **Regenerate** (the old link stops working), and **Cancel**. Once
accepted, the server appears in the subuser's list.

## Adjust or remove access

**Active access** lists everyone with access and their permissions. For a
subuser, toggle the permission chips and select **Save permissions**, or select
**Remove** to revoke access. Removal is immediate. The owner is marked **Owner**
and cannot be removed here.

## Least privilege, always

- Every permission is a way to break something: console access can run
  destructive commands, file access can delete worlds, power access can stop the
  server mid-event.
- Remove subusers who no longer play. Stale access is the most common source of
  "someone griefed my server files" stories.
- Never share your own login instead — then nobody can tell who did what in
  [Activity](/users/activity/), and you cannot revoke access without changing
  your password.

## Related

- [Activity](/users/activity/) — see what a subuser did
- [Roles](/admin/roles/) — how administrators define permission sets
- [Users & Access (admin)](/admin/users/) — panel-wide account management

---

# Tasks

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/tasks/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

The **Tasks** tab (titled **Scheduled Tasks**) runs actions automatically — a
nightly restart, an automatic backup, a timed warning message.

## Prerequisites

- `server.schedule` to see the tab and to create, edit, pause, or delete a task.
- The permission the action itself needs, because a task runs without
  re-checking your rights:
  - **Start server** — `server.start`; **Stop server** — `server.stop`;
    **Restart server** — both.
  - **Create backup** — `backup.create`, plus `server.stop` for **Stop server
    before backup** and `server.start` for **Start server after backup**.
  - **Send command** — `console.write`.

## Create a task

1. Open the server's **Tasks** tab and select **Create task**.
2. Enter a **Name** (the placeholder suggests `Nightly restart`) and, if you
   want a note for your team, a **Description**.
3. Choose the **Action**: **Restart server**, **Start server**, **Stop server**,
   **Create backup**, or **Send command**.
4. For **Send command**, enter the console **Command** — for example
   `say Server restart in 5 minutes`.
5. For **Create backup**, set the backup options:
   - **Stop server before backup** — stops a running server gracefully and waits
     for it to go offline before archiving. Without it the backup only starts
     when the server is already stopped.
   - **Start server after backup** — starts the server again once the backup is
     confirmed finished. Enable both for a backup that restarts the server.
   - **Compress backup (gzip)** — on by default; off stores a plain `.tar`
     ([backups](/users/backups/)).
6. Choose how often it **Repeats**: **Every minute**, **Every N minutes**,
   **Every hour**, **Daily**, **Weekly**, **Monthly**, or **Custom (cron)**.
7. Set the detail the repeat needs: an **Interval** for **Every N minutes**,
   **At minute** for **Every hour**, and a **Time of day** for **Daily**,
   **Weekly** and **Monthly**, plus **Day of week** or **Day of month** where
   they apply. The dialog names the timezone the times are read in.
8. To use a raw cron expression instead, turn on **Advanced** and fill in
   **Schedule (cron)** — five fields: `minute hour day-of-month month
   day-of-week`.
9. Select **Create**.

## Manage existing tasks

Each row shows the name, action, schedule expression, any backup options, and
the **Next run**, **Last run**, status, and **Runs** counters; a failed run
leaves its error text under the row.

- **Edit** opens the name, description, action, command, timing and backup
  options.
- **Pause** keeps a task but stops it running; **Resume** turns it back on.
- **Delete** removes it after a confirmation.

Create, edit, pause and delete are disabled while the server is suspended.

## Recipes that work well

- **Nightly restart:** restart at 04:00 when nobody is online, with a preceding
  **Send command** task (`say Restarting in 5 minutes`) a few minutes earlier.
- **Daily backup:** a backup every night, plus manual backups for milestones.
- **Back up and restart:** one **Create backup** task with **Stop server before
  backup** and **Start server after backup** both enabled — the server stops
  gracefully, the backup is taken, and it starts again once the archive is
  confirmed.
- **Timed messages:** broadcast rules or event reminders with `say`.

## Caveats

- A task action runs with the same power as clicking it yourself — a scheduled
  **Stop server** really stops the server. Name tasks clearly.
- **Start server after backup** only starts a server that the backup left
  stopped; if something else started it while the backup ran, the task leaves it
  alone.
- If the panel was down when a task was due, the task runs when the scheduler
  starts again instead of being skipped. Check **Last run** after an outage.
- A failed run still counts in **Runs** and records its error on the task; a
  task whose node is unreachable fails instead of waiting.
- Over-frequent restarts annoy players and can corrupt worlds if they coincide
  with heavy saves. Daily is plenty for most servers.

## Related

- [Backups](/users/backups/) — manual backups and restoring one
- [Power controls](/users/power/) — starting, stopping, and restarting by hand

---

# Activity

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/activity/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

The **Activity** tab (titled **Activity Log**) is an audit trail for your
server: power actions, file changes, backup restores, subuser changes, and
similar events, each stamped with who did it and when. Entries are a flat list,
newest first, paged 25 at a time. An **Updated …** stamp in the tab header says
when the list last refreshed — hover it for the exact time — and a failed
refresh keeps the entries already on screen, with the error shown above them.

## Read an entry

Each row shows the action, who performed it, the time, and a summary of the
important fields — node, port, or the before/after values a power action
changed. Expand a row's **Details** to see every recorded field. **System**
marks an action the panel took on its own (for example a task or a crash
recovery) rather than one a person triggered.

## Use it for

- **"Who stopped the server?"** — scan for power events and check the actor.
- **"What changed before it broke?"** — correlate the first failure with the
  last file or config change.
- **Subuser oversight** — confirm helpers only touch what they should.

## Limits

- Activity records panel actions, not in-game events. For gameplay history, use
  your game's own logs (see [console](/users/console/)).
- Retention is finite and set by the administrator — 90 days by default. If you
  need a permanent record for a dispute, ask for an audit-log export before it
  ages out.
- If an expected entry is missing, the action may have happened outside the
  panel (direct node access) — ask your administrator.

## Related

- [Console](/users/console/) — in-game history is in the game's own logs
- [Users & Subusers](/users/subusers/) — who has access to your server

---

# Metrics & Alerts

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/metrics/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

The **Metrics** tab shows what your server is actually consuming right now and
over time. The **Alerts** tab on the same server creates rules and lists the
incidents they fire.

## Prerequisites

- A server you can access, with `server.read` for the **Metrics** tab.
- `alert.read` to see alert rules and incidents, `alert.create` to add one,
  and `alert.update` / `alert.delete` to change or remove one. The **Alerts** tab
  also appears with `server.read`, but the rules and history in it need
  `alert.read`.

## Read the Metrics tab

The header shows live detail — memory in use, disk used out of the total, and
received traffic — while the agent is reporting. A stopped server reads zero
CPU and memory rather than showing stale values; if the agent is offline, the
panel keeps the last known values and says so.

Below the header are trend cards for **CPU**, **Memory**, **Disk usage**,
**Disk I/O**, and **Network** (receive plus transmit, in MB/s). The latest value
on each card turns amber past 75% and red past 90% for CPU and memory.

Each card is drawn on a scale that starts at zero — CPU against the whole
allocation, so a line at the top of the card means every allocated core busy —
and small readings keep the decimals they need instead of rounding to nothing: a
server using a fraction of a core reads `0.01 / 4 cores · 0.35% of allocated
cores`, and anything under a hundredth of a core reads `<0.01`. A quiet server
therefore draws a flat line along the bottom of its card rather than a spiky one.

Use the time range selector at the top right to change the window:

- **1 hour**, **6 hours**, **24 hours**, **7 days**, **30 days**.
- **Custom range** — set **Hours** (1–8760) and **Data points** (1–1000).

Next to the selector, an **Updated …** stamp says when the history was last
refreshed; hover it for the exact time.

Gaps in a line mean no sample was recorded for that bucket, not zero usage.

## Read the graphs

- **Memory near the limit with lag spikes:** raise the server's memory (ask your
  administrator) or reduce view distance, plugins, and loaded chunks.
- **CPU pinned at 100%:** a single-threaded game (like Minecraft) saturates one
  core; spread load or upgrade the node allocation.
- **Disk climbing steadily:** logs and backups accumulate — prune `logs/` and
  old backups ([backups](/users/backups/)).
- Compare against quiet hours: if usage is high with zero players, something
  (a farm, a runaway task, a leak) is burning resources.

## Create an alert rule

1. Open the server's **Alerts** tab.
2. Select **Create Rule**.
3. **Details:** give the rule a **Rule name** and optional **Description**,
   choose a **Rule type**, and confirm the **Target**. On a server page the
   target is fixed to that server.
4. **Conditions:** set the thresholds for the rule type:
   - **Resource threshold** — **CPU threshold (%)**, **Memory threshold (%)**,
     and **Disk threshold (%)**. Leave one blank to ignore it.
   - **Node offline** — **Offline threshold (minutes)**.
   - **Server crashed** — no threshold; the rule fires on a crash event.
5. **Notifications:** add **Webhook URLs** (a Discord webhook URL is a common
   choice), **Email recipients**, and optionally tick **Notify server owner**.
   Set the **Cooldown (minutes)** — the minimum gap between notifications from
   the same rule (default 5).
6. Select **Create rule**.

Resource thresholds are checked against the most recent metrics sample: the rule
fires as soon as a reading is over the threshold, and the cooldown stops it from
re-notifying on every check. The **Alert history** section lists incidents with
their severity, the rule that fired, any delivery result (for example a failed
webhook), and a **Resolve** button. Use the filter to show **Unresolved**,
**Resolved**, or **All**.

Alert fatigue is real: alert on symptoms that need action (offline, disk nearly
full), not on every wiggle.

## Where alerts appear

- **Alerts** tab (this page) — rules and incidents scoped to one server.
- **Admin → Alerts** — administrators see every rule and incident with its
  target (**Global**, **Server**, or **Node**), an overview count, and
  **Resolve all**.

## Related

- [Power controls](/users/power/) — what to do when a restart is the fix
- [Admin monitoring](/admin/monitoring/) — node and panel-wide health for administrators
- [Panel issues](/troubleshooting/panel/) — when metrics stop reporting

# Your Account

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/users/account/
Audience: user
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Your Catalyst account is the login you use across the panel. Everything on this
page lives under **Profile**, the user card at the bottom of the sidebar.

## Prerequisites

- A panel account, provided by your host or administrator.
- Access to the email address on the account, for password resets and email
  verification.

## Sign in

1. Open the panel URL, enter your **Email** and **Password**, and select
   **Sign in**. Tick **Remember me** to stay signed in on this browser.
2. If the panel offers it, use **Sign in with passkey**, or **Continue with
   WHMCS** / **Continue with Paymenter** when your administrator enabled them.
3. If the account uses two-factor authentication, enter the code from your
   authenticator app (or a backup code) and select **Verify**. Tick **Trust this
   device for 30 days** to skip the code on this browser.
4. If your administrator requires email verification, sign-in is blocked until
   you confirm your address — the panel tells you to check your inbox for the
   verification link.

## Change or reset your password

**Change it** while signed in:

1. Open **Profile** and find the **Password** card.
2. Enter your **Current password** and a **New password**, and tick **Sign out
   all other devices** if other sessions should be revoked.
3. Select **Update Password**.

An account created through external sign-in has no password yet; the card offers
**Set Password** instead.

**Reset it** when you cannot sign in:

1. On the sign-in page, select **Forgot password?**.
2. Enter your **Email address** and select **Send reset link**. For security the
   panel shows the same confirmation whether or not the address exists — check
   your inbox and spam folder.
3. Open the link, enter a **New password** and **Confirm new password**, then
   select **Reset password**. Passwords must be at least 8 characters.
4. If the link has expired, the page says so — select **Request new reset link**
   to start again.

## Verify your email

The email line on **Profile** shows a **Verified** badge once confirmed.
Otherwise select **Verify email** to resend the verification message.

## Two-factor authentication

1. Open **Profile** and find the **Two-Factor Authentication** card.
2. Enter your password and select **Enable 2FA**.
3. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app, or copy the **Manual Key**.
4. Save the **Backup Codes** shown in the dialog — they are displayed once and
   are the way back in if you lose the authenticator.
5. With 2FA on, the card offers **New Codes** (regenerate backup codes) and
   **Disable** (turn 2FA off, with your password).

## Passkeys

1. Open **Profile** and find the **Passkeys** card.
2. Type a name (optional) and select **Add**. Your browser or device prompts for
   the passkey.
3. Select **Rename** to change the label, or the delete button to remove one.

## Active sessions

The **Active Sessions** card lists every device signed into your account, with
the browser, operating system, IP address, and when it was last active.

- The revoke button on a row signs that device out.
- With more than one session, **Sign Out All Other Devices** revokes the rest.

## Personal API keys

The **API Keys** card lists the keys you created; **Manage API Keys** opens the
API Keys page. Viewing that page needs `apikey.read` (or an admin grant);
creating a key needs `apikey.write` (or `admin.write`).

1. Select **Create API Key**.
2. Give the key a **Name** and choose an **Expiration** — 7, 30, 90 (the
   default), 180 days, 1 year, or **Never expires**.
3. Choose the key's **Permissions**, or leave **All my permissions** selected to
   inherit everything you hold. A key can never exceed your own permissions.
4. Set the **Rate Limit** if the default of 100 requests per minute is wrong.
5. Select **Create API key** and copy the value immediately — it is shown once
   and cannot be retrieved later.
6. **Revoke key** from the list when it is no longer needed; anything using it
   loses access at once.

For what a key can call, see the [API overview](/api/overview/).

## Profile and preferences

- **Avatar:** click the avatar and choose an image (JPEG, PNG, GIF, or WebP), or
  select **Remove avatar**.
- **Name:** select the pencil to edit your **Username**, **First name** and
  **Last name**.
- **Appearance:** sets your theme mode and accent colors for this browser only.
  The **Language** selector in the same card changes the panel interface language
  and is saved to your account, so it follows you to another browser.
- **Linked accounts:** link or unlink WHMCS / Paymenter when your administrator
  has enabled them.
- **Recent Activity:** your recent account actions.
- **Danger Zone:** **Export My Data** downloads
  `catalyst-account-export.json`; **Delete Account** removes the account after
  you type `DELETE` to confirm.

## Related

- [Users & Subusers](/users/subusers/) — giving other people access to your server
- [SFTP](/users/sftp/) — the SFTP password is a separate token, not your panel password

# Overview

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/overview/

Last verified: 2026-10-20

This guide is for the people who run Catalyst itself: installing the panel,
adding nodes, and keeping the whole thing healthy.

## Path for a new operator

1. Check [requirements](/admin/requirements/) — OS, CPU, memory, disk, network.
2. [Install Catalyst](/admin/installation/) with the released installer — one
   `curl` command on a root shell.
3. Complete [first-time setup](/admin/first-time-setup/) — admin account, panel
   name, public URL, and appearance.
4. [Install a node](/admin/nodes/installing/) and [register it](/admin/nodes/registering/)
   — [nodes overview](/admin/nodes/overview/) explains what they do.
5. [Create users and roles](/admin/users/) for your staff.
6. Import or create [templates](/admin/templates/), then make the first server.
7. [Install plugins](/admin/plugins/) if you need extensions.

  [disaster recovery](/admin/disaster-recovery/)
