# Requirements

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/requirements/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## Panel host

- **OS:** Ubuntu/Debian, RHEL/CentOS/Rocky/Alma, Fedora, Arch, Alpine, or
  openSUSE — the distributions the installer knows how to set Docker up on.
- **Architecture:** `linux/amd64` or `linux/arm64`. Panel images are multi-arch
  from release **v1.71.0** onward; on an older release an arm64 host fails to
  pull with `no matching manifest for linux/arm64/v8`.
- **Docker** with the Compose v2 plugin (or **Podman** with `podman compose`).
  The installer can install Docker for you when it is missing.
- **Resources:** roughly 4 GB RAM and 20 GB free disk for the panel, PostgreSQL,
  and Redis. The bundled stack limits the backend to 2 GB, nginx to 512 MB, and
  Redis to 512 MB; PostgreSQL is unbounded. The installer warns when fewer than
  5 GB are free under the install directory.
- **Dependencies:** `curl`, `tar`, and `openssl` on the host — the installer
  stops if any is missing.
- **Network:** a public IP or LAN address, plus a DNS name if you want TLS
  (recommended — see [installation](/admin/installation/)), and outbound HTTPS
  to pull container images. A host firewall must allow the panel port.

## Node hosts

Each node runs game servers through the Catalyst agent (containerd-based):

- **OS:** Linux with systemd (or OpenRC on Alpine).
- **Architecture:** `x86_64`/`amd64` or `aarch64`/`arm64` — the agent installer
  stops on any other architecture.
- **Kernel and cgroups:** cgroup v2 with the **`io` controller** available to
  the agent, and permission to mount loop devices. The agent uses both: the `io`
  controller for per-server IO weight, and loop-mounted disk images for
  per-server disk quotas.
- **Missing either one does not block the node.** Without loop mounts (an
  unprivileged LXC container, for example) the agent falls back to plain data
  directories and **disk quota is not enforced**; without the `io` controller it
  skips the container's IO weight. See [node issues](/troubleshooting/node/).
- **Resources:** whatever your game servers need, plus headroom for the agent
  and the OS. CPU and memory are the usual bottlenecks; disk fills up with
  backups and images.
- **Network:** stable connectivity back to the panel (the agent calls home —
  nodes do not need public IPs unless players connect directly to them).
- Root access for the agent installer.

**Note**
Sizing is workload-dependent: a handful of small Minecraft servers fits on a
4-core/16 GB node, while modded servers and many slots need substantially more.
Start with headroom and watch [monitoring](/admin/monitoring/).

## What you do not need yet

PostgreSQL, Redis, Caddy/Traefik — the Docker installer provisions all panel
dependencies. You only configure them when you outgrow the defaults
([configuration](/admin/configuration/)).

## Related

- [Installation](/admin/installation/) — install the panel once the host meets these.
- [Nodes overview](/admin/nodes/overview/) — how the agent uses cgroups and loop devices.
- [Monitoring](/admin/monitoring/) — watch the resources you sized for.

---

# Installation

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/installation/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

The supported path is the released Docker installer: one command installs
Docker if needed, downloads the compose stack, and writes a fully configured
`.env` with generated secrets. It does **not** start the stack.

## Prerequisites

The full host baseline is on [requirements](/admin/requirements/). In short:

- A supported Linux host: Ubuntu/Debian, RHEL/CentOS/Rocky/Alma, Fedora, Arch,
  Alpine, or openSUSE. RHEL 10 and Fedora 41+ ship dnf5 and the installer
  detects it; RHEL 8/9 still use dnf4.
- `curl`, `tar`, and `openssl` (the installer stops if any is missing).
- Docker with the Compose v2 plugin (or Podman with `podman compose`), or
  permission for the installer to install Docker for you.
- Root access — the one-liner below runs the installer through `sudo bash`.
- If the host runs `firewalld` or `ufw`, the panel port must be open — the
  installer checks it and prints the command.

## Install

On the panel host, from a root shell:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sudo bash
```

The installer reads its prompts from `/dev/tty`, so the piped form stays
interactive. It checks the container runtime and Compose, offers to install
Docker when missing, warns when a port it needs is already in use or disk space
is low, then prompts for the panel URL and panel name. It generates every
required secret (`POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, `REDIS_PASSWORD`,
`API_KEY_SECRET`, `BACKUP_CREDENTIALS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`) and writes `.env` with
`chmod 600`.

On `firewalld` and `ufw` hosts it also reports whether the panel port
(`FRONTEND_PORT`, `8080` by default) is allowed and prints the one-line command
to allow it — advisory only, it never changes the host firewall. If you accept
the HTTPS offer it writes `DOMAIN` and `ACME_EMAIL`, switches `PUBLIC_URL` to
`https://<domain>` and sets `NODE_ENV=production`.

To pin a specific release instead of tracking the newest one, swap `latest` for
a tag (this pins the installer script; the stack files still come from `main`
unless you also set `INSTALL_VERSION`):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst/releases/download/v1.85.0/install.sh | sudo bash
```

### Verify the download (recommended for production)

Every release publishes `install.sh` plus an `install.sh.sha256`. Download both,
check the checksum, then run the file:

```bash
VERSION=v1.85.0  # the release you want
curl -fsSL -o install.sh        "https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst/releases/download/${VERSION}/install.sh"
curl -fsSL -o install.sh.sha256 "https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst/releases/download/${VERSION}/install.sh.sha256"
sha256sum -c install.sh.sha256 && sudo bash install.sh
```

Passing `INSTALL_SHA256=<hash>` makes the script verify itself while it runs (the
raw hex or a whole `.sha256` line both work); a mismatch aborts before anything
happens. The self-check hashes the script file, so it does not apply to the piped
one-liner above.

## Options

Run `--help` for the full list. Useful flags:

- `-y`, `--yes`, `--non-interactive` — accept defaults / use environment
  overrides without prompting.
- `--set KEY=VALUE` — set any `.env` variable (repeatable). Applied on top of
  the prompts, so it also overrides the environment. Secret-looking values are
  never echoed.
- `--env-file FILE` — read `KEY=VALUE` overrides from a file, applied before
  `--set` (a later `--set` wins).
- `--dry-run` — show what would happen without changing anything.
- `--reconfigure` — re-run the `.env` prompts (existing secrets are preserved
  so they stay in sync with already-initialized volumes).
- `--update` — refresh the compose stack files in `./catalyst-docker`, keeping
  `.env`.
- `--uninstall` — remove the stack (data volumes are kept unless
  `REMOVE_VOLUMES=1` is set with `-y`).

Environment overrides (used with `-y`, or as prompt defaults):

- `PUBLIC_URL`, `APP_NAME` — pre-answer the prompts.
- `REMOVE_VOLUMES=1` — with `--uninstall -y`, also delete compose volumes.
- `INSTALL_VERSION` — git ref for the stack files. Defaults to `main`; a
  release tag such as `v1.85.0` pins `catalyst-docker/` to that release so a
  verified installer from release X installs stack X.
- `INSTALL_SHA256` — expected checksum of `install.sh` itself (see above).

Example — non-interactive, pinned stack files, custom port and timezone:

```bash
INSTALL_VERSION=v1.85.0 bash install.sh -y \
  --set PUBLIC_URL=https://panel.example.com \
  --set FRONTEND_PORT=0.0.0.0:8081 \
  --set TZ=Europe/Berlin
```

The installer also records the absolute path of the compose directory in
`CATALYST_COMPOSE_DIR` (bind-mounted at the same path into the backend), which
is what lets the in-panel updater run `docker compose` — see
[updating](/admin/updating/).

## Start the stack

The installer configures the stack but does not start it. Review the generated
`.env`, then bring it up:

```bash
cd catalyst-docker
nano .env   # optional — check everything the installer wrote
docker compose up -d
```

If you answered the HTTPS offer during install (so `PUBLIC_URL` is `https://…`),
start the Caddy overlay instead — it issues the certificate and needs ports
80/443 reachable:

```bash
cd catalyst-docker
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.caddy.yml up -d
```

Check the containers are up with `docker ps`, then open the panel URL in a
browser.

## Finish setup in the browser

Opening the panel URL shows the setup wizard — panel name, admin account, and
appearance ([first-time setup](/admin/first-time-setup/)). The wizard creates the
first account with the **Administrator** role and marks it verified; there is no
separate "first user becomes admin" step.

## After installing

- [Configure TLS and networking](/admin/networking/).
- [Install a node](/admin/nodes/installing/) — the panel alone runs no games.
- [Update safely](/admin/updating/) when new releases arrive.
- `catalyst-docker/diagnose.sh` collects a redacted support bundle;
  `catalyst-docker/update.sh` refreshes the stack files later.

## Troubleshooting

- Installer fails early: re-run with `--dry-run` to see the planned steps, and
  check Docker/Compose are present and your user can reach the Docker socket.
- Port warnings during install: something is already listening on a port the
  stack wants — stop that service or set the matching `*_PORT` variable
  (for example `--set FRONTEND_PORT=0.0.0.0:8081`).
- Panel unreachable from another machine but fine on the host: the host firewall
  is blocking the panel port. Run the `firewall-cmd` or `ufw` command the
  installer printed.
- Panel 500s on first login: the database migrations run at container startup —
  wait a minute and check container logs (`docker compose logs backend`).
- More: [panel issues](/troubleshooting/panel/).

---

# First-Time Setup

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/first-time-setup/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

After [installation](/admin/installation/), opening the panel URL shows the
setup wizard. It runs once and locks itself afterwards. The wizard has three
steps.

## Prerequisites

- A completed [installation](/admin/installation/) with the stack running.
- The panel URL reachable in a browser.
- The backend has finished its startup migrations (otherwise the panel shows a
  **Retry** screen instead of the wizard — see **If the wizard does not appear**
  below).

## Complete the wizard

1. **Welcome.** Set the **Panel Name** (default `Catalyst`) and confirm the
   **Public Panel URL**, which is prefilled with the address you opened the
   panel from. It drives sign-in links, CORS, and generated URLs, so it must be
   the exact URL users open — the same value the installer wrote to
   `catalyst-docker/.env`. The wizard stores it as a panel setting (a database
   override applied on the next panel restart); it does not edit `.env`.
   Optionally upload a **Panel Logo** (recommended: square, at least 128×128px,
   maximum 512KB). Select **Next**.
2. **Admin Account.** Create the first administrator:
   - **Email** — used for notifications and recovery.
   - **Username** — at least 3 characters.
   - **Password** and **Confirm Password** — at least 8 characters. A strength
     meter shows how the password scores.
   Use a strong, unique password. This account is created with the
   **Administrator** role and marked verified automatically.
3. **Appearance.** Pick a **Seed Color** and a **Color Harmony** rule; the
   wizard generates a full palette with a **Live Preview**. Choose whether the
   default theme is **Dark** or **Light**. Select **Complete Setup**.

The wizard signs you in and opens the dashboard. If your browser cannot keep
the new session cookie (common behind a reverse proxy), it sends you to the
sign-in page instead — sign in with the account you just created.

**Note**
Completing setup also switches **open self-registration off** and creates the
built-in **Administrator** and **User** roles. To allow public sign-ups again,
set `REGISTRATION_ENABLED=true` in **Admin → Environment**
([configuration](/admin/configuration/)).

## Immediately afterwards

1. **Verify login works** in a private window (catches cookie/proxy issues early).
2. **[Install a node](/admin/nodes/installing/)** — without one you cannot create servers.
3. **[Create roles](/admin/roles/)** for staff before inviting people.
4. **[Configure backups](/admin/backups/)** for the panel database itself.

**Caution**
The setup wizard is single-use. If you need to re-run it (for example, after
restoring a database), see [disaster recovery](/admin/disaster-recovery/)
rather than deleting data to force it.

## If the wizard does not appear

- You see the login page instead: setup already completed — sign in.
- You see a **Retry** screen: the panel could not reach the backend (a restart
  or update, typically). It keeps checking on its own and recovers when the
  backend answers; select **Retry** to check immediately. An installed panel is
  never sent back to the wizard because a status check failed. See
  [panel issues](/troubleshooting/panel/).

## Related

- [Installation](/admin/installation/) — install the stack first.
- [Installing a node](/admin/nodes/installing/) — the next step after setup.
- [Roles](/admin/roles/) — create staff roles before inviting people.

---

# Updating Catalyst

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/updating/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## Prerequisites

- The panel is running from the bundled Docker stack for the in-panel updater;
  a standalone install uses the manual path below.
- A pre-update database backup — this is the rollback for everything except node
  agents ([backups](/admin/backups/)).
- Administrator access to **Admin → System** (`admin.write`).

## The order (always)

1. **Read the release notes.** Note breaking changes, migration steps, and
   minimum versions.
2. **Back up the database** ([admin backups](/admin/backups/)).
3. **Update the panel** (below). Database migrations run automatically at
   backend startup.
4. **Verify the panel**: log in, open a server console, check a backup listing.
5. **Update nodes one batch at a time** ([updating a node](/admin/nodes/updating/)).

## Update the panel from the UI

When Catalyst runs from the bundled Docker stack, the panel updates itself.

1. Open **Admin → System** and find the **Auto Updater** section. It shows the
   **Current version**, the **Latest version**, and an **Update status** badge.
   If a release is available it reads **Update available**; otherwise
   **Up to date**.
2. Select **Trigger Update**. A **Panel update** dialog opens and streams the
   live log: **Downloading update**, then **Restarting services**. The panel
   goes down briefly and reconnects on its own; the page reloads into the new
   version when it finishes.
3. If the dialog shows **Update failed**, open the panel's **System Errors**
   page (or collect a
   [diagnostics bundle](/troubleshooting/diagnostics-bundle/)) for the reason
   before retrying.

The button is only enabled when the panel detects it is running in Docker and a
newer release exists. On a standalone install the section shows
**Auto-update is only available when running in Docker. Please update Catalyst
manually.** — use the manual path below.

### Automatic updates

The **Auto Updater** section also controls the panel's own automation, and these
settings are stored in the database — they apply immediately, with no redeploy:

- **Panel update automation** — poll for new releases.
- **Install panel updates automatically** — apply a release without confirming.
  Leave this off when you want to read the release notes first.
- **Check for updates** — how often the panel polls (1 hour to 24 hours).
- **Check now** — poll immediately, for when you do not want to wait.

`AUTO_UPDATE_ENABLED`, `AUTO_UPDATE_AUTO_TRIGGER`, and `AUTO_UPDATE_INTERVAL_MS`
only seed these values on the first read; once you save a change in the panel,
the panel wins.

Automatic **node** updates are opt-in per node in the same section — see
[updating a node](/admin/nodes/updating/#automatic-node-updates).

## Update the panel manually

From the directory that holds your stack (`catalyst-docker/`):

```bash
cd catalyst-docker
bash update.sh                 # refreshes compose/nginx/TLS stack files, keeps .env
docker compose pull            # fetch the new images
docker compose up -d           # recreate containers; migrations run at startup
```

`update.sh --dry-run` shows what it would change before touching anything.
`update.sh` upgrades the stack **files** only — the `docker compose pull` step
is what actually moves you to the new image.

If you run the installer with `--update` from the parent directory, it delegates
to the same script:

```bash
bash install.sh --update
```

Watch the backend logs until migrations finish (`docker compose logs -f backend`).

## Rules

- Pin production to release tags, not `main`. Track `main` only in a lab.
- If the panel fails to start after an update, read the container logs before
  doing anything — most failures are a migration waiting on a lock or an env
  variable renamed in the release notes.

## Rollback

- Panel: restore the database backup, then restart the previous images.
- Nodes: reinstall the previous agent build on the affected node.
- After any rollback, repeat the four verification checks above.

## Recovering from a failed migration

The backend runs `prisma migrate deploy` on every container start
(`catalyst-backend/docker-entrypoint.sh`). If a migration fails, the entrypoint
logs `migrate deploy failed`, refuses a destructive `db push` (unless
`ALLOW_DATA_LOSS=1` is set) and starts the backend anyway — which then errors at
runtime on the missing schema. Recover in this order.

1. **Take a dump first**, even if the panel is down — the pre-update backup is
   the supported rollback ([disaster recovery](/admin/disaster-recovery/)).
2. **Read the failure.**
   ```bash
   docker compose logs backend | grep -A 20 -i migration
   ```
3. **Inspect the migration table** for the row that never finished:
   ```bash
   docker compose exec catalyst-postgres psql -U catalyst -d catalyst_db
   ```
   ```sql
   SELECT migration_name, started_at, finished_at, rolled_back_at
   FROM "_prisma_migrations"
   ORDER BY started_at DESC
   LIMIT 5;
   ```
   A row with `finished_at` NULL and `rolled_back_at` NULL is the failed
   migration.
4. **Fix the cause, then re-run.** Most failures are a transient lock, a
   version/env mismatch, or a full disk. Once fixed, recreating the backend
   re-runs the deploy:
   ```bash
   docker compose up -d backend
   docker compose logs -f backend
   ```
5. **If it still fails, restore the pre-update dump** and redeploy the previous
   release. That is the rollback the panel supports.

**Caution**
Never edit or delete an already-applied migration, and do not hand-edit
`_prisma_migrations`. If a migration must be re-applied after a correction, use
Prisma's own `prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back <name>` from inside the
backend image — then redeploy. Setting `ALLOW_DATA_LOSS=1` makes the entrypoint
fall back to `prisma db push --accept-data-loss`, which can drop columns; use it
only on a throwaway database.

## Related

- Panel and node update order: this page and [updating a node](/admin/nodes/updating/).
- Pre-update database dump and restore: [disaster recovery](/admin/disaster-recovery/).
- Backup schedule and storage: [backups](/admin/backups/).
- Update failures at runtime: [troubleshooting](/troubleshooting/overview/).

---

# Overview

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/nodes/overview/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

A node is a Linux machine that runs game servers. The panel never runs games
itself — it tells nodes what to run, and the **agent** on each node does it.

## Lifecycle

1. **Register** — create the node in the panel and copy the install command it
   shows ([registering a node](/admin/nodes/registering/)).
2. **Install** — run that command on the machine; the agent connects back to the
   panel ([installing the agent](/admin/nodes/installing/)).
3. **Allocate** — define the IP addresses and port ranges servers may use, so
   they get join addresses.
4. **Operate** — create servers on it, watch health, and apply agent updates
   ([updating a node](/admin/nodes/updating/)).
5. **Retire** — migrate servers off, then remove the node.

Registering comes first on purpose: the panel issues the credential the agent
authenticates with, so the node record must exist before you run anything on the
machine.

## How panel and node communicate

- The **agent calls the panel** (outbound HTTPS/WebSocket). Nodes do not need
  inbound panel ports — useful behind NAT.
- Players connect **directly to the node** on game ports.
- If the link drops, running servers keep running; the panel shows the node as
  unreachable until the agent reconnects. See
  [node issues](/troubleshooting/node/).
- The agent reports its version on every check-in. When the panel is newer, the
  node's page flags an update and offers **Update Agent**.

## Capacity thinking

Nodes are divided by memory first, CPU second, disk third. Overcommitting
memory causes the worst failures (the kernel kills game processes), so keep
headroom and set per-server limits honestly. Node-level over-allocation is a
percentage you set when registering: `0` disables it and `-1` treats capacity as
unlimited. [Monitoring](/admin/monitoring/) shows when a node is full before your
players notice.

## Related

- [Registering a node](/admin/nodes/registering/), [installing a node](/admin/nodes/installing/), and [updating a node](/admin/nodes/updating/).
- [Node requirements](/admin/requirements/) — kernel, cgroups, and disk quota.
- [Administrator guide](/admin/overview/) — where nodes fit in.

---

# Registering a Node

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/nodes/registering/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Registration introduces a machine to the panel: identity, credentials, and the
network addresses it may hand out to servers. Do it before installing the agent,
because the panel is what issues the agent's credential.

## Prerequisites

- Administrator access — registering a node needs the `node.create` permission
  (a role with `admin.write` also passes).
- The target machine meets the [node requirements](/admin/requirements/).
- The node's hostname and public address (an IPv4 or IPv6 literal) to hand.
- A location to group the node under; you can create one in the dialog.

## Register the node

1. Open **Admin → Nodes** and select **Register Node**. The dialog is a single
   screen with numbered sections and a live summary of what you are about to
   create.
2. **1 — Location**: where the node physically sits. If no locations exist yet,
   select **Create a location**, then come back and pick it.
3. Fill in the remaining sections — **Node details**, **Connection**,
   **Capacity**, and **Advanced agent paths**:

   | Field | Required | Notes |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | **Name** | Yes | Datacenter + purpose, for example `eu-frankfurt-01`. |
   | **Description** | No | Free text shown in the node list. |
   | **Server data directory** | Pre-filled | Where server files live on the node. Default `/var/lib/catalyst/servers`. |
   | **Hostname** | Yes | How the panel reaches the agent. |
   | **Public address** | Yes | Address players connect to — an IPv4 or IPv6 literal. |
   | **Memory (MB)** | Yes | Total memory the node may allocate. Default `16384`. |
   | **CPU cores** | Yes | Total CPU cores the node may allocate. Default `8`. |
   | **Memory Over-allocation (%)** | No | `0` = none, `-1` = unlimited. |
   | **CPU Over-allocation (%)** | No | Same meaning. |
   | **SFTP Access** | No | On by default, port `2022`. Change it later in **Update node**. |
   | **Advanced agent paths** | No | Container-runtime and CNI paths. Leave blank to use agent defaults. |

4. Select **Register node**. The panel creates the node record and its ID.
5. The dialog switches to **Deploy agent** and shows the install command, which
   carries a new agent API key. Select **Copy** and run it on the machine —
   [installing a node](/admin/nodes/installing/) covers the details. Select
   **Done** to close the dialog.

The node's first check-in flips it to online in **Admin → Nodes**. If you lose
the command, open the node and select **Deploy** to generate a fresh one.

## Add allocations

Servers need IP + port pairs. Open the node and select **Allocations**, then use
the **Port Allocations** tab → **Create Allocations**. Enter one or more IPs and
one or more ports; the field accepts a single value (`25565`), a range
(`25565-25664`), or a comma-separated list.

- Only add IPs actually configured on the node.
- Reserve panel/agent/management ports — never hand them to game servers.
- For dedicated-IP (MACVLAN) networking, create an **IP Pool** instead; each
  server then takes one IP from the pool automatically.

The node's **Allocations** page also shows how many allocations are assigned and
free, so you can see when a node is running out.

## Credential hygiene

- The agent API key is a long-lived secret issued with the install command and
  shown only there. If one leaks, rotate it: open the node, select **Regenerate
  Key**, and update `/opt/catalyst-agent/config.toml` on the node.
- One key per node — never copy a key between machines.
- The deployment token in the install command's URL is single-use and expires
  after 24 hours; the API key in the command does not expire.

## Related

- [Installing a node](/admin/nodes/installing/) — run the deploy command the panel shows.
- [Updating a node](/admin/nodes/updating/).
- [Node issues](/troubleshooting/node/).

---

# Installing a Node

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/nodes/installing/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Create the node entry in the panel first, then run the install command the
panel gives you on the machine that will host it. That one command installs
everything the node needs — the container runtime, the agent, its configuration
and the service — so a fresh machine needs nothing pre-installed.

## Prerequisites

- A Linux machine meeting the [requirements](/admin/requirements/) with root
  access (the command uses `sudo`).
- The node entry created in the panel — see
  [registering](/admin/nodes/registering/). The panel issues the install
  credential for that node, so it must exist first.
- The node can reach the panel's URL. The agent calls home over a WebSocket, so
  the node does not need a public IP or an inbound panel port.
- Outbound HTTPS from the node to fetch the container runtime and the agent
  binary.

## Install the agent

1. In the panel open **Admin → Nodes**, select **Register Node**, and fill in
   the dialog ([registering](/admin/nodes/registering/)). Give the node its
   hostname, public address, and the memory/CPU capacity of the machine.
2. After you select **Register node**, the same dialog switches to **Deploy
   agent** and shows the node's install command:

   ```bash
   curl -fsSL -H 'Authorization: Bearer <API key>' 'https://panel.example.com/api/deploy/<deployment token>' | sudo bash -x
   ```

3. Select **Copy** and run that command **on the node machine** as a user with
   `sudo`. The `-x` prints a shell trace to stderr, which is what you want if the
   install stops partway.
4. Wait for `Installation complete!`. The script prints the node ID, the config
   path, and the log command.

**Caution — The install command is a credential**
The URL embeds a deployment token that is single-use and expires after 24 hours;
the `Authorization` header carries a long-lived agent API key. Run the command
over a trusted channel and do not paste it into tickets, chat, or shell history
on a shared machine. If the token is consumed or expires before you run it, open
the node in the panel and select **Deploy** to generate a fresh command.

### What the command installs

The panel's command is a short bootstrap: it writes the API key to a `0600` file
so it never appears in the process list, fetches the node installer from the
panel, and runs it with the key in `CATALYST_API_KEY_FILE`. The command also
pins `AGENT_VERSION` to the panel's own version, so the node installs the exact
agent version that panel understands. The installer then:

- Detects the package manager (`apt`, `dnf`, `yum`, `pacman`, `zypper`, `apk`)
  and the init system (systemd, or OpenRC on Alpine).
- Installs and enables containerd — the container runtime the node runs game
  servers through — plus the CNI plugins used for server networking.
- Downloads the agent binary **matching the panel's version**: from GitHub
  Releases first, then from the panel itself if GitHub is unreachable.
- Writes `/opt/catalyst-agent/config.toml` with mode `0600`, containing the
  panel URL and the node API key.
- Installs the `catalyst-agent` service and starts it. The agent then opens its
  own ports in the host firewall it detects (`ufw`, `firewalld`, or
  `ipset`/`iptables`): each server's allocation ports as the server starts, and
  the SFTP port.

## Verify

1. In **Admin → Nodes** the node turns online within a minute.
2. On the node, confirm the service is running:
   - systemd: `systemctl status catalyst-agent`, logs with
     `journalctl -u catalyst-agent -f`
   - OpenRC: `rc-service catalyst-agent status`, logs in
     `/var/log/catalyst-agent.log`
3. Create a test server on the node and start it before offering the node to
   users.

## Re-running and upgrading

Re-running the install command is safe: the installer backs up the existing
configuration as `config.toml.bak.<timestamp>` before rewriting it. To move an
existing node to a newer agent after a panel upgrade, see
[updating](/admin/nodes/updating/).

## Automation: run the installer directly

The panel's command wraps `scripts/deploy-agent.sh` — the same file baked into
the backend image at `/scripts/deploy-agent.sh` and served at
`/api/agent/deploy-script`. Run it directly when you manage the installer
yourself rather than through the panel:

```bash
CATALYST_API_KEY_FILE=/root/node-key deploy-agent.sh <panel_url> <node_id> <node_hostname>
```

- `CATALYST_API_KEY_FILE` keeps the API key out of the process list. Passing the
  key as the third argument also works, with the hostname as the fourth.
- `AGENT_VERSION=x.y.z` pins the agent version instead of asking the panel.
  Without it the installer queries the panel (`/api/agent/version`) and installs
  the matching version.
- `AGENT_RELEASE_REPO` changes where the binary is fetched from.
- `DATA_DIR` (default `/var/lib/catalyst`), `CONSOLE_LOG_DIR`, `SFTP_PORT` and
  the `CNI_DIR` / `CNI_BIN_DIR` / `CNI_DATA_DIR` / `CNI_RESULTS_DIR` /
  `CNI_BRIDGE_NAME` / `CNI_BRIDGE_SUBNET` variables override the defaults
  written into the configuration.

## If it fails

Work through [node troubleshooting](/troubleshooting/node/). The usual causes
are: the node cannot reach the panel URL, the deployment token was already used
or expired, the distribution is unsupported by the installer, or the machine
lacks a kernel feature the container runtime needs. The installer's output and
the `catalyst-agent` logs on the node say which step failed.

## Related

- [Registering a node](/admin/nodes/registering/) — create the node entry first.
- [Updating a node](/admin/nodes/updating/) — move an installed node to a newer agent.
- [Node issues](/troubleshooting/node/) when the agent will not come online.

---

# Updating a Node

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/nodes/updating/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

The panel drives agent updates: it reports the agent version each node is
running and, once the panel is newer, offers an **Update Agent** command that the
agent applies to itself. Running game servers keep running while the agent
restarts and reconnects. Nothing is updated automatically unless you approve the
node first (see [automatic node updates](#automatic-node-updates)).

## Prerequisites

- The panel is already on the target version — a node only updates to the
  version the panel itself runs ([updating Catalyst](/admin/updating/)).
- The node is online; the update command travels over the agent's WebSocket.
- Administrator access (`admin.write`) to trigger the update.

## Safe update order

1. **Update the panel first** ([updating Catalyst](/admin/updating/)). The agent
   update targets the panel's own version, so a newer panel is what makes the
   node update available.
2. Update **one node** and watch it for a full day before touching the rest.
3. Update remaining nodes in batches, never all at once.

## Automatic node updates

The panel does **not** push agent updates to every outdated node. Each node is
either **Automatic** or **Manual**:

- **Manual** (default) — the node keeps its current agent version. The panel
  flags **Update available** and you run the update yourself.
- **Automatic** — when the panel's agent version is newer than the node's, the
  panel sends the update command on its own.

Choose the mode in **Admin → System → Auto Updater → Automatic node updates**:
tick the nodes you trust to update unattended, untick the rest, then select
**Apply**. Selecting rows only stages the change — nothing is sent until you
apply, and the count badge shows how many nodes are currently automatic.

A node that is offline, or currently mid-update, is skipped; it is picked up on
the next health report once it can take the command. A node is only ever updated
to the version the panel itself runs.

Start with a canary: approve one node, watch it for a full day, then approve the
rest. To update a Manual node now, use the per-node steps below.

## Update one node from the panel

1. Announce maintenance — the agent restarts during the update.
2. Open the node in **Admin → Nodes**. If its agent is behind the panel, the
   header shows a version badge (`v<current> → v<latest>`) and the **Update** tab
   carries a status dot.
3. Open the **Update** tab and compare **Current** with **Latest**. Select
   **Update Agent**. The button is only enabled when the panel has a newer
   version; when there is nothing to do it reads **No Update**.
4. Watch the status in the same panel: it moves through `downloading` (with a
   progress bar) and `restarting`, then clears. A failure shows the error text.
5. Verify: the node is healthy again, a test server starts, the console streams,
   and backups list.

The panel sends the update over the agent's WebSocket, so the node must be
online — an offline node reports "Failed to send update command to agent". The
agent downloads the binary (GitHub Releases first, panel as fallback), verifies
its checksum, swaps the binary in with an atomic rename, and restarts itself.
A download or checksum failure aborts before anything is replaced.

## Node settings are a different dialog

The header's settings button opens **Update node**, which edits the node's
identity, capacity, SFTP, and agent paths — not its version. Changes there apply
to future deployments and do not restart the agent. To re-run the install command
with new paths, use **Deploy** on the node header.

## Rules

- Never update the panel and all nodes simultaneously. A bad release then breaks
  everything instead of one canary node.
- Game servers themselves do not update with the agent — game versions come from
  templates ([templates](/admin/templates/)).
- Keep a changelog note per node (agent version + date) for the next incident.

## Related

- [Updating Catalyst](/admin/updating/) — panel first, nodes after.
- [Installing a node](/admin/nodes/installing/) — re-running the deploy command.
- [Nodes overview](/admin/nodes/overview/) — version reporting and check-ins.
- [Node issues](/troubleshooting/node/) when a node will not reconnect.

---

# Configuration

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/configuration/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Most day-to-day settings live in the panel UI. A handful of infrastructure
variables must be set in the compose environment before the backend starts;
everything else can be managed from the panel.

## Change a setting in the UI

This is always the first place to look. Every screen below validates input and
saves immediately — except **Admin → Environment**, which asks for a restart
when a change needs one.

| Screen | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| **Admin → System** | SMTP email, mod manager API keys (CurseForge/Modrinth), default interface language, and **Auto Updater** |
| **Admin → Security** | Rate limits, email verification, lockout policy, file-upload limits, and the panel MCP endpoint |
| **Admin → Environment** | Every environment variable the backend reads, with its source and a restart prompt when required |
| **Admin → Theme** | Panel identity (panel name, logo, favicon), brand colors, surfaces, and custom CSS |
| **Admin → Databases** | MySQL hosts used to provision databases for servers, plus Catalyst database health |
| **Admin → Plugins** | Installed plugins: permissions, configuration, enable/disable, updates |
| **Admin → Marketplace** | The **Plugin marketplace** (`/admin/plugins/marketplace`) — browse and install from the configured sources |
| **Profile** | Your own language, password, passkeys, and API keys |

## Mod manager API keys

**Admin → System → Mod Manager API Keys** stores the keys the Mod Manager uses
to search and download mods, datapacks and modpacks. Keys are write-only in the
panel: once saved, only the last four characters are shown.

1. Open **Admin → System**, section **Mod Manager API Keys**.
2. Paste the key into **CurseForge API Key** and/or **Modrinth API Key** and
   save.
3. Ask a user to open the Mod Manager tab and confirm the provider appears in
   the provider selector.

CurseForge requires a key for every request. Modrinth is hidden from the
provider selector when its key is empty, so an unconfigured Modrinth key looks
exactly like "the provider does not exist" rather than an error. If a user
reports that a provider is missing from the Mod Manager, check this section
first.

A key shared by many servers is rate limited by the provider; heavy use shows
up as search returning fewer results or downloads failing intermittently.

## Environment variables in the panel

**Admin → Environment** renders the backend's own registry
(`catalyst-backend/src/lib/env-registry.ts`): every variable it reads, with its
category, where the current value comes from (**Environment**, **Database** or
**Default**), and whether a restart is needed. A value saved there is stored in
the database and applied on the next panel start — the page offers a **Restart
panel** button, and **Reset to .env** drops the override.

Variables that have a dedicated editor are hidden from this page so each value
has one home: the panel name under **Theme**, rate limits and console output
under **Security**, update automation under **System → Auto Updater**, OIDC
providers under **Theme → Advanced**, and marketplace sources in the
**Marketplace** page.

Six variables are read before the backend can reach the database, so they are
**`.env` only** (shown read-only in the panel): `DATABASE_URL`, `NODE_ENV`,
`PORT`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, `TZ`, and `WORKERS`. `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`,
`REDIS_PASSWORD`, and `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` are also the values the containers
themselves start with, so change them in `.env` and recreate the stack:

```bash
cd catalyst-docker
nano .env
docker compose up -d
```

## Environment reference

`catalyst-docker/.env.example` is the annotated template the installer copies.
Docker ports, as written by the installer: `FRONTEND_PORT=0.0.0.0:8080`,
`BACKEND_PORT=127.0.0.1:3000`, `POSTGRES_PORT=127.0.0.1:5432`. With no `.env`,
compose falls back to `FRONTEND_PORT=0.0.0.0:80`. **Redis is
published on `127.0.0.1:6379` (loopback only)** — the compose default
`REDIS_PORT` is `127.0.0.1:6379`, and commenting it out does not unpublish the
port. To make Redis fully internal to the Docker network, add a `ports: []`
override for the `redis` service. See [networking](/admin/networking/).

`PUBLIC_URL` is the single source of truth for the panel URL — it drives CORS,
auth origins, and email links, and the installer derives `PASSKEY_RP_ID` from
its hostname. [networking](/admin/networking/) covers the TLS and proxy side.
Re-run the installer's prompts to regenerate a configured `.env` with
`bash install.sh --reconfigure` ([installation](/admin/installation/)).

`NODE_ENV` (`development`, `production`, `test`; default `development`) and
`SUSPENSION_DELETE_POLICY` (`block` or `allow`) are enum-validated at startup: a
wrong value exits the backend with `Invalid environment configuration`.
`LOG_LEVEL` reaches pino only when `NODE_ENV=production` (otherwise `info`), an
unrecognised `BACKUP_STORAGE_MODE` silently falls back to `local`, and a
malformed `PUBLIC_URL` breaks CORS, auth origins, and email links at runtime
instead of at startup. The suspension policy applies only while suspension is
enforced, and only `DELETE /api/servers/:id` compares it literally — unset means
deletion is allowed. The admin bulk delete uses `SUSPENSION_DELETE_BLOCKED`
instead, which defaults to blocking.

**Note**
If the backend exits at startup with `Invalid environment configuration`, the
`[config] Environment variable validation failed` lines above it name the
variable. `SUSPENSION_DELETE_POLICY=keep` — the commented value in
`catalyst-docker/.env.example` — is **not** accepted; use `block` or `allow`.

## Rules

1. **Do not edit the database by hand.** Every supported change has a UI field,
   an API endpoint, or a documented variable. Raw SQL edits bypass validation
   and break upgrades ([updating](/admin/updating/)).
2. **Keep secrets out of chat and screenshots.** Database passwords, API keys,
   and node tokens live in your compose `.env`, never in docs or tickets.
3. **Record what you changed.** A one-line note (what, when, why) saves hours
   during the next incident.

## Related

- Database and cache tuning: [storage](/admin/storage/).
- TLS and proxy headers: [networking](/admin/networking/).

---

# Networking

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/networking/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## Panel access (HTTPS)

Serve the panel behind **Caddy** (automatic certificates) or **Traefik**. Both
ship as overlay compose files in `catalyst-docker/`; you layer one on top of the
base stack with `-f`.

For Caddy, the fastest path:

1. Set a DNS A record pointing your domain at the panel host.
2. In `catalyst-docker/.env`, set `DOMAIN=panel.example.com` (required) and
   `ACME_EMAIL=admin@example.com` (optional, for certificate notifications).
3. Start the stack with both files:

   ```bash
   cd catalyst-docker
   docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.caddy.yml up -d
   ```

Caddy obtains and renews the Let's Encrypt certificate, redirects HTTP → HTTPS,
and proxies to the frontend. Ports 80 and 443 must be reachable from the
internet for the ACME challenge — the overlay publishes them as
`HTTP_PORT=0.0.0.0:80` and `HTTPS_PORT=0.0.0.0:443`.

For Traefik, use `docker-compose.traefik.yml` the same way. It discovers the
frontend through Docker labels and exposes its dashboard on
`TRAEFIK_DASHBOARD_PORT` (`127.0.0.1:8080` by default).

Terminating TLS at the proxy and running the panel behind it over plain HTTP is
the normal layout — but then only the proxy may reach the panel port. The
overlays remove the frontend's direct host exposure; if you use `podman-compose`
(which merges port lists instead of replacing them), also set
`FRONTEND_PORT=127.0.0.1:8080` in `.env` to keep direct access off the public
interface.

`PUBLIC_URL` must be the exact URL users type (scheme + host) — the single
source of truth for CORS, auth, and email links. The installer derives
`PASSKEY_RP_ID` from its hostname. See [configuration](/admin/configuration/)
for the full environment reference.

## Node ↔ panel

Agents call home over HTTPS/WebSocket, so nodes need **outbound** access to the
panel URL. No inbound holes toward nodes are required for management. If a node
shows unreachable while its servers run fine, the management path (DNS, proxy,
panel) is broken — not the games. See [node issues](/troubleshooting/node/).

## Game traffic

Players connect directly to nodes, so each game port in your allocations must
be reachable from the internet (or your LAN). UDP matters — many games use UDP,
and a TCP-only test will mislead you.

The agent opens the ports itself: when a server starts it allows the server's
allocated ports through the firewall it detects (`ufw`, `firewalld`, or
`ipset`/`iptables`) and removes them when the server is deleted. On `firewalld`
it writes both the runtime and the permanent rule, so the port is reachable
immediately and survives a reboot, without reloading the daemon. Anything in
front of the node — a cloud security group, an upstream NAT — is still yours to
configure. The panel port is the one thing nobody opens for you: the installer
checks `firewalld`/`ufw` and prints the command
([installation](/admin/installation/)). Debugging steps live in
[networking issues](/troubleshooting/networking/).

## SFTP

SFTP is served by the node agent, not the panel — the default port is `2022`.
The per-node port is set in **Admin → Nodes** and written into the agent's
config; the agent opens it on the node's firewall when it starts.

## Checklist for a new site

1. DNS → panel, TLS valid, login works in a private window.
2. Node checks in healthy.
3. A test server's game port answers from outside your network.
4. SFTP port reachable if you offer it to users.

## Related

- Environment reference and where to change variables: [configuration](/admin/configuration/).
- Game-port and firewall troubleshooting: [networking issues](/troubleshooting/networking/).
- Node reachability and the agent connection: [nodes overview](/admin/nodes/overview/).

---

# Storage

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/storage/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## Panel host

The bundled stack keeps four named Docker volumes: `catalyst-postgres-data`
(the database), `catalyst-server-data`, `catalyst-backup-data` (backups), and
`catalyst-plugin-data`.

- **PostgreSQL** is the system of record — users, servers, audit logs, settings.
  Back it up continuously; see [backups](/admin/backups/) and
  [disaster recovery](/admin/disaster-recovery/).
- **Backups** are stored in the `catalyst-backup-data` volume
  (`/var/lib/catalyst/backups`) by default. Choosing the storage backend
  (`BACKUP_STORAGE_MODE`) and its retention is covered in
  [backups](/admin/backups/).
- **Redis** is an ephemeral cache and coordination layer: config caches,
  cross-instance invalidation, realtime fan-out, agent command relay, shared
  rate-limit counters, and locks. It has **no volume, no AOF/RDB, and no
  persistence by design** — sessions live in PostgreSQL, not Redis. Losing
  Redis means slower requests and degraded realtime, never lost data; the
  backend falls back to the database when it is down
  (`catalyst-backend/src/lib/redis.ts`).
- Keep database volumes on fast, monitored disks separate from bulk backup
  storage.

## Nodes

Each server's data lives in a per-server loop-mounted disk image whose size is
the server's disk allocation — that is how Catalyst enforces a per-server disk
quota. A node that cannot mount images (an unprivileged LXC, for example) falls
back to plain data directories with **no quota enforcement**
([requirements](/admin/requirements/)).

Node disk fills with, in rough order: game server images and data, container
images, logs, and temporary backup staging. Plan for it:

1. **Separate filesystems** (or at least quotas) for server data vs. images/logs,
   so a log flood cannot wedge game I/O.
2. **Image pruning** on a schedule — old game images accumulate silently.
3. **Backup retention** that matches disk. The agent stages each archive under
   its data root before it is transferred to the panel, S3, or SFTP, so large
   backups still need node headroom.
4. **Alert at 80%, act at 90%.** A full disk stops servers ugly. Wire node disk
   into [monitoring](/admin/monitoring/).

## Rules

- Never let any volume hit 100%. Ever. This is the single most preventable
  cause of "everything broke at 3 AM".
- Test restores, not just backups — an untested snapshot is a hope.

## Related

- Backup backend, retention, and restore-testing: [backups](/admin/backups/).
- Rebuilding the panel after disk loss: [disaster recovery](/admin/disaster-recovery/).
- Node kernel and disk-quota requirements: [requirements](/admin/requirements/).
- Watching disk usage before it fills: [monitoring](/admin/monitoring/).

---

# Users

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/users/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Manage accounts under **Admin → Users**.

## Prerequisites

- The `user.create` permission (or full administrator access) to create accounts.
- At least one [role](/admin/roles/) defined if you want to assign one at
  creation time.

## Create an account

You need `user.create`. Select **Create user** and fill in the numbered
sections of the form:

1. **Account credentials** — **Email**, **Username**, and **Password** (at
   least 8 characters).
2. **Roles & Servers** — assign one or more **Roles** (the chips are
   multi-select and searchable) and, optionally, direct server access.
3. **Node Access** — grant the account scoped access to specific nodes, or skip.
4. Select **Create user**.

**Edit user** reopens the same form with a fourth **Security** section for the
account's two-factor, passkey, and linked-account state; leaving the password
blank keeps the current one. Saving needs `user.update`; changing roles also
needs `user.set_roles`.

## Find and act on users

- Search by name, email, or ID, and filter by **Role** or **Status** (**Active**,
  **Banned**, **Unverified**).
- **View details** shows the account, its roles, sign-in history,
  **Two-Factor Authentication**, **Passkeys**, and **Linked Accounts** state.
  The actions live in **Edit user**'s **Security** section: **Wipe 2FA**, **Wipe
  all** passkeys, **Enforce** or **Unenforce** 2FA, and **Unlink** an SSO
  account.
- Unverified accounts get a **Verify email** action on their row and in the
  row's overflow menu.
- Select users to act in bulk: **Ban**, **Unban**, **Verify Emails**, or delete.
  Banning and deleting are destructive; a user who still owns servers cannot be
  deleted.

Server sharing between players does **not** need admin help — owners send
invites and add [subusers](/users/subusers/) themselves from the server's
**Users & Access** view.

## Admin discipline

1. **Few admins.** Admin rights bypass every limit in the system. Most staff
   need a scoped [role](/admin/roles/), not admin.
2. **Named accounts only.** No shared `admin` login — shared logins make the
   audit log useless and revocation impossible.
3. **Offboard promptly.** **Ban** the account when staff leave; sessions are
   revoked and the account's API keys stop authenticating.
4. **Strong auth.** Enforce strong passwords and enable the MFA/SSO options in
   [security](/admin/security/).

## When users cannot log in

1. Confirm the account exists and is not banned; check **Status** in
   **Admin → Users**.
2. Set a new password by editing the user (leave the password blank to keep the
   current one), or **Verify email** from the user's row if the address is
   unverified.
3. Check mail delivery if invites or resets never arrive (see
   [panel issues](/troubleshooting/panel/)).
4. In **Admin → Audit Logs**, filter the action `login_failed` (shown as
   **Sign-in failed**) or the resource type `auth_lockout` (**Login lockout**)
   before resetting anything.

## Related

- Designing least-privilege roles: [roles & permissions](/admin/roles/).
- Account security settings: [security](/admin/security/).
- What owners can share themselves: [subusers](/users/subusers/).

---

# Roles & Permissions

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/roles/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

**Roles** are named bundles of permissions; users get powers through roles, not
one-off grants. Manage them under **Admin → Roles**.

## Prerequisites

- The `role.create` permission (or full administrator access).
- A clear idea of the job the role serves — see **Design principles** below.

## Create a role

The role editor is one screen with three sections — **Role details**, **Where
this role applies**, and **What members can do** — plus an **Effective access**
summary that updates as you change them.

1. Open **Admin → Roles** and select **Create role**.
2. **Role details** — set a **Name** (for example `Support L1`) and an optional
   **Description**.
3. **Where this role applies** — pick one access boundary: **Panel
   administration** (panel-wide permissions only, no node or server access),
   **Entire panel** (every server on every node, including ones added later),
   **Selected nodes** (every server hosted on those nodes), or **Specific
   servers**. Search and tick the nodes or servers you mean.
4. **What members can do** — leave the **Wildcard — All Permissions** switch off
   and tick individual permissions, or start from a preset (**Administrator**,
   **Moderator**, **Support**, **User**) and adjust it; **Clear** empties the
   selection. The search box filters by name. Permissions are split into
   **Resource permissions** — granted only inside the boundary you chose — and
   **Panel-wide permissions**, which are always global. Permissions that
   installed plugins expose for roles appear in a **Plugins** group.
5. Select **Create role** (or **Save changes** when editing). The role is listed
   immediately; assign it to a user under **Admin → Users**.

**Node access** — which nodes members can reach at all, independent of the
boundary above — is assigned after the role exists: edit the role and use the
**Node access** block.

**Edit role** reopens the same editor. A role that still has assigned users
cannot be deleted; remove or reassign those users first.

The **Wildcard — All Permissions** switch grants every current and future
permission panel-wide and clears the boundary. Roles that hold it show a **Full
Admin** badge in the list and **Full Administrator Access** in the detail view;
do not hand that out casually.

## Design principles

1. **Least privilege.** Start from nothing and add what the job needs. It is
   easy to grant more later; it is hard to un-see leaked data.
2. **Job-shaped roles.** `Support L1` (view servers, restart, read logs),
   `Billing` (view users, no server control), `Node operator` (nodes only).
   Avoid one giant `Staff` role.
3. **Separate read from write.** Most incidents come from write access that was
   only ever needed for reading.
4. **Review quarterly.** Roles accrete permissions; audit who has what and trim.

## API keys follow the same model

Admin-created [API keys](/api/authentication/) carry scoped permissions from
the same catalog — a monitoring key gets read-only metrics, not server control.
The exact strings are listed in
[Authorization & Permissions](/api/authorization/#permission-catalog), served by
`GET /api/roles/permissions-catalog`.

## Dangerous combinations

- User management + server file access can become full account takeover paths.
- Backup restore + subuser creation can exfiltrate other users' data.
- When a role needs a risky permission, time-box it: grant, do the task, revoke.

## Related

- Creating and assigning users: [users](/admin/users/).
- Scoped API keys using the same permission catalog: [API authentication](/api/authentication/).
- Built-in security controls and lockouts: [security](/admin/security/).

---

# Security

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/security/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## Panel

- Serve everything over HTTPS with valid certificates ([networking](/admin/networking/)).
- Keep the panel updated — security fixes ship in releases ([updating](/admin/updating/)).
- Restrict who can reach the admin UI by network (VPN, allowlist) in addition
  to passwords.
- Never expose the database or Redis ports to the internet; the bundled compose
  stack binds both to loopback ([configuration](/admin/configuration/)).

## Accounts and access

- Few admins, named accounts, prompt offboarding ([users](/admin/users/)).
- Least-privilege [roles](/admin/roles/) for staff; scoped
  [API keys](/api/authentication/) for integrations.
- Treat node API keys and backup encryption keys as crown jewels: generated
  randomly, stored once, rotated on suspicion.

## Security settings

Open **Admin → Security**. Settings take effect when you select **Save** in
each section.

- **Rate Limits** — per-category request and message budgets: **Auth requests**,
  **File operations**, **Console input**, **Console output lines / sec**,
  **Console output bytes / sec**, **Agent messages / sec**, **Agent metrics /
  sec**, **Server metrics / sec**, and **Max buffer (MB)**. Each rate limit has
  a count and a time window (second, minute, hour, day, or month).
- **Email Verification** — **Require verified email before sign-in**. The toggle
  is disabled until SMTP is configured under **Admin → System**. If a saved
  payload asks for it while mail is not configured, the backend stores it as
  off instead of failing the save, so the other security settings still apply.
- **Lockout Policy** — **Max attempts**, **Window (minutes)**, **Duration
  (minutes)**, and **Audit retention (days)**. Failed sign-ins lock out per
  email + IP combination.
- **File uploads** — **Tunnel requests**, **Max upload size (MB)** (up to
  10240 MB), **Max pending per node**, and **Max concurrent (agent)**. The
  upload size caps a single file in the file browser on every node; SFTP
  transfers are limited only by the server's remaining disk. **Max concurrent**
  needs an agent restart to take effect.
- **Auth Lockouts** — recent lockout entries with a **Clear lockout** action.

Open self-registration is not on this page. It is governed by
`REGISTRATION_ENABLED`, which overrides the stored setting: set it in **Admin →
Environment** and restart the panel ([configuration](/admin/configuration/)).
The setup wizard turns the stored setting off.

## Panel MCP endpoint (AI assistants)

The panel can expose itself as a Streamable HTTP MCP server so an AI
assistant can manage servers, nodes, users, and the rest of the panel API
with the same permissions as the API key it is given. It is **disabled by
default**.

Prerequisites: an admin account, and a panel API key for the assistant
(Profile > API keys) scoped to only the permissions it needs.

1. In **Admin → Security**, find the **Panel MCP access** section.
2. Turn on **Enable panel MCP endpoint**. A confirmation dialog explains the
   risks; select **I understand, enable anyway**. It takes effect immediately —
   no restart.
3. Optionally set the **Tool budget (per key / min)** (10–5000, default 300).
   The **MCP endpoint** field shows the exact URL to copy —
   `https://panel.example.com/api/mcp`.
4. Select **Save**.
5. Point the MCP client at that endpoint with the dedicated API key as the
   Bearer credential.
6. Verify with a read-only call first (for example `whoami`), then try one
   `list_servers` before granting broader scopes.

**Caution**
Destructive tools (delete, reinstall, restore, ban, …) run as soon as the
assistant calls them with `confirm: true`. Use a least-privilege key, keep
the per-minute tool budget low, and revoke the key when the job is done.

Session cookies are never accepted on this endpoint, so it cannot be
abused from a browser session. Every tool call is permission-checked and
audit-logged exactly like direct API use.

## Nodes

- Only the agent's required ports plus game allocations listen publicly.
- Apply OS and runtime updates on a rhythm; nodes run untrusted game code and
  third-party mods by design.
- Review [imported egg install scripts](/admin/importing-eggs/) — they are the
  largest untrusted-code surface in normal operation.

## Report a vulnerability

Do not open a public issue for a suspected security bug. Report it privately to
the maintainers and expect coordinated disclosure: report, fix window, then a
public advisory.

## Related

- [Networking](/admin/networking/) — TLS and proxy layout.
- [Users](/admin/users/) and [roles](/admin/roles/) — account and permission hygiene.
- [Updating Catalyst](/admin/updating/) — ship security fixes promptly.
- [Importing eggs](/admin/importing-eggs/) — the untrusted-code boundary.

---

# Templates

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/templates/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

**Templates** define installable games: container image, install script,
startup command, variables, and defaults. Users pick a template when creating a
server; everything else flows from it. Manage them under **Admin → Templates**.

## Prerequisites

- The `template.create` permission, or full administrator access.
- A [node](/admin/nodes/overview/) if you want to install-test the template
  before publishing it.

## Add a template

From **Admin → Templates**:

1. Select **New Template**. One dialog holds every field, in numbered sections:
   **1 — Nest** (the nest that groups the template, or **Skip — no nest**, plus
   **Name**, **Author**, **Version**, **Icon URL**, and **Description**),
   **2 — Runtime images**, **3 — Commands & config** (startup command, stop
   command or signal, the optional **Install script**, config file paths, and
   **Resources & ports**: **Ports**, **Allocated memory (MB)**, **Allocated CPU
   cores**), **4 — Variables**, and **5 — Advanced features**.
2. Select **Create template**. Until the required fields are filled the footer
   lists what is missing and the button stays disabled. The template is then
   available immediately and users can create servers from it.

To bring in an existing game definition instead, select **Import** on the same
page ([importing eggs](/admin/importing-eggs/) walks through the whole flow):

- **From URL** — paste a direct link to a Pterodactyl egg (`.json`/`.yaml`).
- **From Local File** — **Choose file** on your computer.
- **Import All Pterodactyl Eggs** — imports the full `pterodactyl/game-eggs`
  collection and creates nests from the egg categories. This takes a minute or
  two.

Imported templates carry a primary port derived from the egg itself (its `ports`
array, a literal port in the egg's config-file bindings, or a variable pinned to
one value) rather than assuming 25565. Eggs that only bind
`{{server.build.default.port}}` pin nothing, because the panel allocates the
real port per server — check **Ports** before publishing those.

## Verify before you publish

A template you have not installed from scratch is untested. Create a real
server from it, install, start, join, stop, back up, and restore. Only then
offer it to users.

## Maintain templates

- **Edit** on a template card opens the same form; **Save changes** applies
  immediately to future servers.
- **Pin versions** in install scripts where stability matters; `latest` moves
  under you on the worst possible day.
- **Keep variables minimal.** Every variable is support surface — expose what
  users actually change, hide the rest in sane defaults.
- **Note behavioural changes.** Existing servers usually keep their old
  effective config until they are reinstalled, so say whether users must act.
- **Retire broken templates.** Select them and use the bulk delete action; a
  template in use by an existing server cannot be deleted.

## Nests

Nests group templates (Minecraft, Source, and so on). Keep the nest list short
and obvious — it is the first choice users make, and twenty near-identical
entries help nobody.

Select **Nests** on the Templates page to open **Manage nests**, then **New
nest**; give it a **Name**, optional **Description**, and optional **Icon URL**.
Deleting a nest leaves its templates ungrouped rather than deleting them.

## Related

- Importing Pterodactyl eggs and nests: [importing eggs](/admin/importing-eggs/).
- What users see when they create a server: [creating a server](/getting-started/first-server/).
- Migrating whole servers: [migration](/admin/migration/).

---

# Importing Pterodactyl Eggs

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/importing-eggs/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Catalyst can import Pterodactyl eggs as templates, so a library built for
Pterodactyl does not have to be rebuilt from scratch. Imports live on the
[templates page](/admin/templates/) (**Admin → Templates**), not in the
migration center — that page imports whole servers. Both JSON (Pterodactyl) and
YAML (Pelican) eggs work.

## Prerequisites

- The `template.create` permission, or full administrator access.
- For **From URL**, outbound access from the backend to the egg's host.
- For **Import All Pterodactyl Eggs**, outbound access from the backend to
  GitHub.

## Import one egg

1. Open **Admin → Templates**.
2. Select **Import**.
3. Choose **From URL** and paste a direct link to the egg file, or **From Local
   File** and pick a `.json`, `.yaml`, or `.yml` file.
4. The panel converts the egg and opens the **New template** form pre-filled.
   Review the name, nest, runtime images, startup command, variables, ports, and
   install script.
5. Select **Create template**.

Selecting several files at once on the local-file route skips the review step and
creates each template directly — a single file opens the editable form.

## Import the whole Pterodactyl library

1. Open **Admin → Templates** and select **Import**.
2. Under **Import All Pterodactyl Eggs**, select **Import All** (the button
   shows how many eggs it will fetch). The panel warns this may take 1–2 minutes
   while it fetches the eggs from GitHub.
3. The result reports how many templates were imported, skipped (already exist),
   and failed. Expand **Error details** to see which eggs failed and why.
4. **Nests are created automatically** from the egg categories in the repository,
   so the imported library arrives pre-grouped.

## Organize the imported templates

Nests are the template categories, and the batch import creates them from the
repository's egg folders. Add, rename, or delete nests under **Manage nests** on
the Templates page ([templates](/admin/templates/#nests)).

## What to check by hand

- **Ports:** the template's primary port is derived from the egg — an explicit
  `ports` array, a literal port in the egg's own config-file bindings, or a
  variable pinned to one value by its rules — instead of assuming 25565. Eggs
  that bind `{{server.build.default.port}}` pin nothing, because the panel
  allocates the real port per server; those templates fall back to 25565 as a
  placeholder, so correct the **Ports** field before publishing.
- **Variables:** names, defaults, and validation rules sometimes need renaming
  to match Catalyst conventions.
- **Images:** confirm the container image exists and is maintained; repoint to
  your own registry mirror if you run one.
- **Install scripts:** read them. Imported scripts run as part of installation
  with significant privilege — never import eggs from sources you do not trust.
- **Paths:** document root and config paths occasionally differ; a quick
  install test exposes this immediately.

**Caution**
Imported install scripts execute code from the egg author. Review every script
before publishing its template to users — this is a supply-chain boundary.
See [security](/admin/security/).

## Automation

The batch button calls `POST /api/templates/import-pterodactyl-batch`; a single
egg can be posted as JSON to `POST /api/templates/import-pterodactyl`. Both
require the `template.create` permission and return structured validation errors
(422) for eggs that cannot be converted. Full-panel migrations import nests and
templates on their own — see [migration](/admin/migration/).

## Related

- Creating and maintaining templates: [templates](/admin/templates/).
- Moving whole servers: [migration](/admin/migration/).
- Why imported install scripts need review: [security](/admin/security/).

---

# Plugins

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/plugins/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Plugins extend the panel with new pages, server tabs, API routes, scheduled
work, and sign-in providers. Manage them under **Admin → Extensions**. A plugin
runs in the panel process with the access you grant it, so every install is a
trust decision — see [security](/admin/security/).

## Prerequisites

- `admin.read` to browse, `admin.write` to install, enable, or change anything.
- Outbound HTTPS from the backend to the marketplace index and the package
  host. Loopback and private addresses are refused unless the host is one of
  your configured index hosts or the panel sets
  `PLUGIN_MARKETPLACE_ALLOW_LOCAL=true`.
- For a vendor-licensed plugin, the license key from the vendor.

## Install a plugin

1. Open **Admin → Extensions → Marketplace**.
2. Browse the configured sources. The status tabs filter to **All**, **Install**,
   **Update**, and **Installed**; expand a row for its author, source,
   checksum, package URL, homepage, and licensing block.
3. Select **Install**. A package is a `.catpkg.zip` — a ZIP whose root contains
   `plugin.json`.
4. Installed code is staged **inert**. It is not imported and none of its hooks
   run until you accept the safety disclaimer and enable it.

Installing over an existing copy upgrades it in place. The same flow over the
API needs a pinned checksum:

```bash
curl -X POST https://panel.example.com/api/plugins/install \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CATALYST_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"https://cdn.example.com/my-plugin-1.0.0.catpkg.zip","sha256":"<64 hex chars>"}'
```

`sha256` is **required**: the panel validates the 64-hex digest before it makes
any network request (`CHECKSUM_REQUIRED`), and aborts before extracting if the
downloaded bytes do not match (`CHECKSUM_MISMATCH`). An index entry without a
digest shows **Not published** and cannot be installed.

The marketplace merges the official index (unless
`PLUGIN_MARKETPLACE_DISABLE_OFFICIAL` is set), comma-separated
`PLUGIN_MARKETPLACE_URLS`, and sources added from the panel. Add, enable, or
remove panel-added sources in the marketplace's **Marketplaces** rail; the
official and environment sources are read-only. When two sources list the same
plugin name, the newest version wins.

## Enable a plugin and accept the safety disclaimer

Nothing in a plugin executes before an accepted disclaimer — discovery only
reads `plugin.json`.

1. In **Admin → Extensions → Plugins**, switch the plugin on.
2. The **Enable** dialog lists the author, version, every declared permission
   with its risk copy, and — for a licensed plugin — the activation endpoint it
   will contact. It warns that a plugin can contact external services, read the
   data permitted above, and keep running until you disable it.
3. Tick the acknowledgement and select **Accept & Enable**. The panel records
   who accepted, when, which version, and which permissions were in scope.

Consent is required again when the plugin's version changes, when its declared
permissions grow beyond the accepted set, or when the disclaimer version
changes. Re-enabling an unchanged plugin does not ask again. An update that
changes either is left **disabled** after the copy lands (reload included)
until you accept the new disclaimer.

A plugin that was already enabled before this feature existed keeps starting:
the panel records a backfill acceptance with no accepting user and flags the row
**Review access**.

Disabling a plugin makes its routes answer `503` and clears its scheduled work
and WebSocket handlers. Event listeners stay registered until the plugin is
unloaded (reload or uninstall).

## Grant and revoke plugin permissions

A plugin declares the capabilities it wants in `plugin.json`; you decide which
it receives. Open the plugin's **Details** → **Permissions**, toggle, save.
Grants must be a subset of the declared list, and every change is audit-logged.

Revocation applies to the next call: data reads, file operations, and
plugin-to-plugin calls fail immediately, with no restart. Mounted routes,
scheduled work, and event listeners stay until you disable or unload the plugin.

Plugins can also expose permissions for panel **roles** (a separate namespace
from the plugin's own capabilities). While a plugin is enabled they appear in
the role editor under **Plugins** — see [roles](/admin/roles/).

## Configure a plugin

Open the plugin's **Settings**, fill in the fields its config schema declares,
and save. The running plugin reads the new values immediately. The control type
comes from each field's `type`; see
[config field types](/api/plugins/manifest/#config-field-types). The panel
validates nothing on save, so a plugin must check what it reads.

## Update, reload, disable, uninstall

- **Version column** — the installed version, plus the marketplace version when
  it is newer (an `Update 1.0.0 → 1.0.1` badge), or **Up to date** /
  **Not in an index**.
- **Update** — installs the newer listing over the running copy. The list header
  shows **N updates available**, which links to the marketplace filtered to
  pending updates, where **Update all (N)** applies them one at a time.
- **Reload** — re-reads the plugin from disk without restarting the panel, and
  leaves it disabled if the new copy needs consent.
- **Disable** — stops the plugin; its files and settings stay installed.
- **Uninstall** — removes the code and unloads it. **Also delete stored data**
  additionally removes config values, key-value storage, collections, and
  consent history, and cannot be undone.

## Licensing

Catalyst does not issue or validate plugin licenses. A vendor plugin declares a
`licensing` block in `plugin.json`; the panel discloses the phone-home before
you enable it, hands the plugin a stable install ID, and refuses to install a
package marked `encrypted` that ships no encrypted backend payload.

Put the vendor's license key in the plugin's config (usually `licenseKey`) and
reload it. Activation is cached in the plugin's own storage (7 days by default),
so a vendor outage does not immediately take the plugin down; when activation
fails the plugin degrades or fails according to its declared `failMode`. See
[plugin licensing](/api/plugins/licensing/).

## Related

- Least-privilege roles and plugin-exposed permissions: [roles & permissions](/admin/roles/).
- Trust boundaries and hardening: [security](/admin/security/).
- Building a plugin: [plugin development](/api/plugins/).
