# Backups

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/backups/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Two different things need backing up, with different tools and rhythms. The
panel and its database are the operator's job; each server's files are the
owner's — but the storage backend and retention rules are set here.

## 1. The panel database

PostgreSQL holds users, servers, roles, audit logs — everything except the game
files themselves. If it is gone, the fleet is unmanageable. The exact `pg_dump`
and restore commands live in [disaster recovery](/admin/disaster-recovery/);
this page owns the schedule and the fleet-wide storage settings.

- Take automated dumps on a schedule (daily minimum) and ship them off the
  panel host.
- Retain enough history to survive a weekend discovery (7–30 days is typical).
- **Restore-test quarterly** into a scratch environment
  ([the recovery drill](/admin/disaster-recovery/)).

## 2. Choose the fleet-wide backup backend

Backups are stored by the backend; pick the default in the panel's `.env`
(the file the installer wrote next to `docker-compose.yml`) and apply it:

```bash
# edit .env, then:
docker compose up -d backend
```

```bash
BACKUP_STORAGE_MODE=local   # local | s3 | stream | sftp
```

- **local** (default) — files under the backend's backup directory
  (`BACKUP_DIR`, `/var/lib/catalyst/backups` in the Compose stack).
- **s3** — an S3-compatible bucket. Also set `BACKUP_S3_BUCKET`,
  `BACKUP_S3_REGION`, `BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY`, `BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY`, and
  optionally `BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT` / `BACKUP_S3_PATH_STYLE=true`.
- **stream** — the agent streams each archive to the panel's scratch directory
  (`BACKUP_STREAM_DIR`), useful when no persistent backup volume is mounted.
- **sftp** — upload to a per-server SFTP target, configured on the server.

All four modes are selectable in **Admin → Environment**. Values outside them
fall back to `local`.

Set `BACKUP_CREDENTIALS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (32-byte base64, e.g.
`openssl rand -base64 32`) before storing per-server S3 or SFTP credentials —
without it, saving them fails, except outside production with
`ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_CREDS=1`. Rotating the key makes stored credentials
undecryptable.

## 3. Per-server overrides

Each owner manages backups in the server's **Backups** tab, and **Backup
settings** there overrides the fleet default — storage mode, **Keep last N**, and
**Max age (days)**. [User backups](/users/backups/) documents that tab; the
backend enforces retention from a six-hourly job and again inline as each
backup completes.

With **local** or **stream** storage and no **backup allocation**, the create
call fails `403` — *Backup allocation disabled. Configure S3 or SFTP to enable
backups.* **S3** and **SFTP** servers skip that quota entirely.

Pinning needs the `backup.pin` permission (**Pin backups (ignore retention
limit)** in the role editor). Server ownership does not imply it: grant it
through a role ([roles](/admin/roles/)) or to an individual
[subuser](/users/subusers/); `admin.write` and `*` satisfy it too.

## 4. Secondary drive (an extra local copy)

When backup storage lives on the same disk as everything else, a node or disk
loss takes the archives with it. **Admin → System → Secondary backup drive**
adds a second, panel-wide destination — typically a separately mounted disk —
that a finished backup can be copied to.

- **Enable the secondary drive for new backups** is the master switch. Off is
  the default, and with it off the option is hidden in the create dialog and
  the API rejects requests that ask for it.
- **Directory** is an absolute path on the panel host, e.g.
  `/mnt/backup-drive/catalyst`. The directory must already exist; the panel
  never creates it, so an unmounted drive cannot silently fill the root
  filesystem. It must be at least two levels deep and must not overlap
  `BACKUP_DIR`, `BACKUP_STREAM_DIR`, `BACKUP_TRANSFER_DIR` or the server data
  directory.
- Saving with **Enable** ticked validates the path immediately and fails the
  save if the directory is missing, relative, contains `..`, or overlaps a
  managed directory.

With the drive enabled, each owner can tick **Copy to the secondary drive** when
creating a backup. The archive is written to a temporary file inside the
destination and renamed into place once complete, so a half-written copy is
never exposed. Copies apply to **Local** and **Stream** storage; S3 and SFTP
already store off the panel host.

The copy is an extra copy, never a replacement: a failed copy is recorded on the
backup row (and shown as a **Secondary drive copy failed** badge) while the
primary archive stays untouched. Deleting a backup removes its secondary copy
too. Downloading a backup whose node is offline falls back to the secondary copy.

Backup paths are re-validated against the canonical (resolved) destination
directory on every create, read and delete, and symbolic links are refused, so a
crafted backup name or stored metadata value cannot escape the configured
directory. Only an administrator with `admin.write` can read or change the
setting; everyone else only learns whether the option is available.

## Rules

1. **3-2-1:** three copies, two media, one off-site — for the database at least.
   Server backups stored on the same node die with the node; a correctly
   configured secondary drive is the cheapest second copy, but it still sits in
   the same machine room.
2. **Encrypt off-site copies.** Backups contain credentials and private player
   data.
3. **Monitor failures.** A backup task that has errored for a month is the same
   as no backup. Failures surface in the server's **Backups** tab and the panel
   system errors view.

## Related

- Rebuild procedure and the quarterly drill: [disaster recovery](/admin/disaster-recovery/).
- Where backup files live on disk: [storage](/admin/storage/).
- What owners can do themselves: [user backups](/users/backups/).

# Monitoring & Logs

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/monitoring/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## What to watch

| Layer | Signals | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Panel | HTTP errors, login failures, DB/Redis health | **Admin → Overview** (**System Health**), **System Errors** |
| Nodes | Reachability, CPU/memory/disk, agent version drift | **Admin → Nodes**, node detail stats |
| Servers | Crash loops, backup failures, quota usage | **Servers**, per-server **Metrics** and **Backups** tabs |
| Platform | Disk free everywhere, certificate expiry, backup age | Alerts plus your own host monitoring |

The admin dashboard shows **System Health** (**Database**, **Cluster Nodes**)
and the cluster resource chart. Ship the same numbers to your existing
monitoring (Prometheus/Grafana, Uptime Kuma, log shipping) rather than living in
the panel UI.

## System Errors

Open **Admin → System Errors** (`/admin/system-errors`). This is the panel's
own error log: exceptions captured from the backend, agents, and frontend. The
header shows **Live** when the realtime stream is connected (otherwise
**Offline**) plus the current error count.

1. Filter with **Level** (**All levels**, **Warning**, **Error**, **Critical**),
   **Component** (for example `auth, server...`), **Node**, **Status** (**All**,
   **Resolved**, **Unresolved**), **From**/**To**, and **Quick range**
   (**Custom**, **Last 1h**, **Last 6h**, **Last 24h**, **Last 7d**). Active
   filters show as chips; **Clear** resets them.
2. Per row, **View details** opens the stack trace and metadata, **Copy for AI**
   copies a Markdown report, and **Resolve** marks one error handled.
3. **Resolve all** marks every error matching the current filters resolved
   (disabled while you are filtering to resolved errors).
4. **Export** opens a dialog: pick a **Time range** and a **Format** — JSON, or
   Markdown for pasting into an assistant. Up to 5,000 of the most recent
   errors are included.
5. **Download diagnostics** captures panel, node, server, and config data for a
   time window as one redacted ZIP — see
   [diagnostics bundle](/troubleshooting/diagnostics-bundle/).

Triage here first when a page 500s or a background job misbehaves, then read
**Audit Logs** (`/admin/audit-logs`) for who triggered the action. Audit logs
are your source of truth for staff actions; export CSV and protect retention
under **Admin → Security**.

## Set up alerting

1. Open **Admin → Alerts** and select **Create Rule**.
2. **Details** — name the rule, pick a **Rule type**: **Resource threshold**
   (CPU/memory/disk percentages), **Node offline** (offline threshold in
   minutes), or **Server crashed**; choose a **Target** (**Global**, **Node**,
   or **Server**).

**Note**
   **Resource threshold** rules cannot use the **Global** target — the panel
   rejects them at creation with "use target `server` or `node`" because there
   is no fleet-wide aggregation. Pick a specific server or node instead.
3. **Conditions** — set the thresholds the rule type exposes.
4. **Notifications** — add **Email recipients**, **Webhook URLs**, a **Cooldown
   (minutes)**, and optionally **Notify server owner**.
5. Select **Create rule**. Incidents appear under **Alert history**; use
   **Resolve** or **Resolve all** once handled.

At minimum, page on: panel down, node unreachable > 5 min, disk > 85%, and a
panel database backup older than expected. Certificate expiry is not something
the panel watches — track it in your host monitoring. Prune stale rules
quarterly; they train people to ignore the channel.

## Logs that matter

- **Backend container logs** — API errors, auth failures, background jobs:
  `docker compose logs backend`.
- **Agent logs on each node** — lifecycle actions, update stages, connectivity:
  `journalctl -u catalyst-agent`.
- **System errors view** — persisted application errors worth triaging regularly.

## When something fires

Go to [troubleshooting](/troubleshooting/overview/) with the alert text, the
affected host, and a timestamp. Those three facts solve half of all incidents.

## Related

- Per-server resource graphs: [server metrics](/users/metrics/).
- Backup health and retention: [backups](/admin/backups/).
- Node reachability and agent versions: [nodes overview](/admin/nodes/overview/).

# Migration

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/migration/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

The migration center (**Admin → Migration**) imports a Pterodactyl panel into
Catalyst as a tracked job: test the connection first, map the target nodes, then
run. Each job exposes phase- and step-level status, so you can retry a failed
step, pause, resume, or cancel without starting over. Migration requires an
administrator account.

## Prerequisites

- A Catalyst node that is **online** with enough free capacity for the servers
  you are moving. Migration refuses to start with no online target node.
- The source panel's **Application API Key** (`ptla_…`). It must be allowed to
  change server feature limits: when a source server has no backup slots (or all
  of them are used), the job raises its backup limit so it can create the
  migration backup. If that call fails, that server's backup step is skipped.
- The source panel's **Client API Key** (`ptlc_…`) if you want backups, server
  files, schedules and subusers migrated. Without it those steps are skipped.
  Create it in Pterodactyl under **API Credentials → Client API**.
- Templates and nests are imported automatically by the job — you do not have to
  run [egg imports](/admin/importing-eggs/) first, though doing so lets you fix a
  template before a large run.

## Run a migration

1. Open **Admin → Migration**. The **New Migration** tab is the default.
2. Under **Connect**, enter the source **Panel URL** and **Application API Key**,
   plus the optional **Client API Key (for file migration)**.
3. Select **Test Connection**. The panel reports the source's locations, nodes,
   nests, users, and servers, and warns about servers with no free backup slots.
4. Choose the **Migration Scope**:
   - **Full Migration** — every source node, mapped onto Catalyst nodes.
   - **Node by Node** — only the source nodes you select.
   - **Server by Server** — map individual servers to a Catalyst node.
5. Under **Map Pterodactyl Nodes to Catalyst Nodes** (or **Map Pterodactyl
   Servers…** for server scope), pick the target node for each entry. Click an
   entry to preview what will be imported. The scope applies to the whole job,
   so pick one before mapping.
6. Select **Start Migration**. The **Start Migration** button stays disabled
   until the connection test succeeds, every entry required by the scope is
   mapped, and at least one target node is online.
7. The view switches to the **Active Migration** tab. Work the phases top to
   bottom: Validation, Locations, Templates (Nests & Eggs), Users, Servers,
   Subusers, Databases, Schedules, Backups, Server Files. Use **Pause** /
   **Resume** to control the job, **Cancel** to stop it, and the retry button on
   a failed step to re-run just that step. A failed step does not mean a failed
   migration.
8. Finished jobs move to the **History** tab with their step counts.

## Safest order of operations

1. Run the connection test and read the warnings before starting anything; fix
   backup slots or missing keys on the source panel first.
2. Migrate a pilot server (or a small node) and complete the full cycle —
   import, install, start, join, backup, restore — before a large run.
3. Run the rest in batches, during low-traffic windows, biggest risk first.
4. Verify each batch with server owners before moving on.
5. Keep the source panel and servers stopped-but-present until owners confirm.
   The rollback is to turn the old server back on.

## Per-server checklist

- Files and worlds intact (compare sizes and spot-check).
- Databases moved and plugins reconnecting.
- Startup variables and schedules recreated ([tasks](/users/tasks/)).
- Backups running on the new side before DNS or addresses switch.

**Caution**
Do not delete or wipe the source panel while a migration is in progress or
unverified. The migration is one-way; the source is your rollback until owners
confirm the new servers.

## Related

- Importing individual eggs as templates: [importing Pterodactyl eggs](/admin/importing-eggs/).
- Reviewing imported templates before a large run: [templates](/admin/templates/).
- Rolling back a failed panel update: [disaster recovery](/admin/disaster-recovery/).

---

# Disaster Recovery

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/admin/disaster-recovery/
Audience: admin
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## What you must be able to rebuild

1. **Panel database** — users, servers, roles, audit logs: everything except
   the game files. It lives in the `catalyst-postgres-data` volume (Compose
   prefixes the name with the project name).
2. **Panel configuration** — the compose directory the installer created
   (`./catalyst-docker` under the directory you ran it from) with its `.env`.
   The `.env` holds `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`,
   `API_KEY_SECRET`, and `BACKUP_CREDENTIALS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`; losing them
   invalidates sessions, API keys, and stored backup credentials even if the
   database survives.
3. **Node agents** — reproducible: reinstall from the panel with a fresh
   **Deploy** command ([installing a node](/admin/nodes/installing/)). Game data
   comes back from user backups ([user backups](/users/backups/)).
4. **File volumes** — `catalyst-server-data`, `catalyst-backup-data`, and
   `catalyst-plugin-data` on the panel host. Redis has **no** volume: it is an
   ephemeral cache and is rebuilt from the database automatically.

## Back up the panel

Schedule, retention, and the storage backend are covered in
[backups](/admin/backups/); this section is the command reference. Run these on
the panel host, from the compose directory. `POSTGRES_USER` and `POSTGRES_DB`
default to `catalyst` and `catalyst_db`; use your `.env` values, and read
`CATALYST_COMPOSE_DIR` there if you have moved the stack.

```bash
cd ./catalyst-docker                # the directory install.sh created
docker exec catalyst-postgres pg_dump -U catalyst -d catalyst_db \
  > catalyst-panel-$(date +%F).sql
tar czf catalyst-config-$(date +%F).tgz \
  .env docker-compose.yml docker-compose.*.yml nginx caddy traefik
```

To capture the file volumes as well, archive each one with a throwaway
container. Compose prefixes volume names with the project name (the compose
directory name), so discover the real names first:

```bash
docker volume ls --format '{{.Name}}' | grep -E '_catalyst-(server|backup|plugin)-data$' \
  | while read -r v; do
      docker run --rm -v "$v":/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
        tar czf "/backup/${v}.tgz" -C /data .
    done
```

Ship the dump, the config archive, and the file archives off the host. Check
that the dump is non-empty before you trust it.

## Restore the panel

1. On the replacement host, install a fresh stack with the one-liner:
   `curl -fsSL https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sudo bash`
   ([installing Catalyst](/admin/installation/)). Stop it before importing:
   `docker compose down` — never `down -v`, which deletes the volumes.
2. Put the saved **`.env`** back into the compose directory. Restoring the
   original secrets is what makes existing sessions, API keys, and backup
   credentials valid again.
3. Start PostgreSQL only, then restore the dump into it:
   ```bash
   docker compose up -d postgres
   cat catalyst-panel-<date>.sql | docker exec -i catalyst-postgres \
     psql -U catalyst -d catalyst_db
   ```
4. Restore the file volumes, if you captured them. The volume names must match
   the ones Compose expects, which is why the compose directory keeps the same
   name:
   ```bash
   shopt -s nullglob
   for f in catalyst-*_catalyst-{server,backup,plugin}-data.tgz; do
     v="${f%.tgz}"
     docker run --rm -v "$v":/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
       sh -c "rm -rf /data/* && tar xzf /backup/$f -C /data"
   done
   ```
5. Start the rest of the stack: `docker compose up -d`.
6. Log in, open **Admin → Nodes**, and confirm each node reconnects. Nodes that
   were wiped or rebuilt need a fresh agent install; their game data comes from
   backups on the node or in the backup volume.

`bash update.sh --restore <backup-dir>` restores the compose files from the
backup `update.sh` takes before it rewrites them — useful if an update is what
broke the stack.

## Restore failures that are not the archive's fault

A restore that dies partway is usually the node, not the backup. Two known
causes, both fixed in current agent releases — keep nodes updated before
drilling:

- **`Function not implemented` (`ENOSYS`) on Fedora 44.** Fedora's GNU tar uses
  `openat2(2)` when extracting, and systemd's `RestrictSUIDSGID=yes` blocks that
  syscall. The agent unit now ships `RestrictSUIDSGID=no` with the other sandbox
  directives intact, and a node upgraded in place repairs itself on the next
  agent start. See
  [backup restores fail with Function not implemented](/troubleshooting/node/#backup-restores-fail-with-function-not-implemented).
- **Symbolic and hard links in the archive.** Older agents refused them. Current
  agents restore links inside the server directory as they were and still refuse
  archive-supplied ownership, permissions, device entries, and any member or
  link that would escape the server directory.

## The recovery drill (quarterly)

If you have never restored, you do not have recovery. Take a fresh dump, config
archive, and file archive; restore them into a scratch host as above; log in,
open servers, list backups, check the audit log; and time the whole thing — that
duration is your real RTO.

During a real incident: declare who is in charge and where status is posted,
restore in dependency order (database → panel → nodes → verify servers), and
keep the recovery instructions somewhere other than the host they recover.

## Related

- Backup schedule, storage backend, and retention: [backups](/admin/backups/).
- Installing a fresh stack: [installation](/admin/installation/).
- Re-adding nodes: [installing a node](/admin/nodes/installing/).
- User-side restore: [user backups](/users/backups/).

---

# Overview

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/overview/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Catalyst exposes a REST API for everything the panel does, plus realtime streams
for console output, server events, and metrics.

## Start here

1. [Authentication](/api/authentication/) — create an API key and send it as a
   bearer token.
2. [Authorization](/api/authorization/) — the permission model and every
   permission string.
3. [Errors](/api/errors/) — stable codes you can branch on.
4. [Pagination](/api/pagination/) and [rate limits](/api/rate-limits/).
5. [Realtime events](/api/websockets/) — console, server events, metrics.
6. [Guides](/api/guides/) — common workflows end to end.
7. [Plugin development](/api/plugins/) — extend the panel itself.
8. [API reference](/api/reference/) — generated endpoint documentation.

## Conventions

- **Base path `/api`** (for example `/api/servers`, `/api/nodes`), over HTTPS.
- JSON bodies, UTF-8.
- **API keys** are created in the panel and sent as
  `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. A request without that header falls back to
  session-cookie auth.
- **Pagination differs per endpoint** — some use `page`/`limit`, `GET
  /api/servers` uses `limit`/`offset`. Check [Pagination](/api/pagination/)
  before writing a generic page walker.
- Errors carry a stable machine-readable `code` in addition to the message —
  branch on the code, never on English text.

## Source of truth

The [API reference](/api/reference/) is generated from the backend's route
definitions, so it tracks the code. The same document is served raw at
`/openapi.json`. If a guide here disagrees with the reference, the reference and
the actual behaviour win — report the mismatch so the guide gets fixed.

---

# Authentication

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/authentication/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## Two credential types

| Credential | For | How it is sent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Session** | The panel UI and browser flows | Session cookie |
| **API key** | Scripts, bots, integrations | `Authorization: Bearer <key>` header |

Use API keys for anything programmatic — do not automate logins or scrape
session cookies. `Authorization: Bearer` is the only header the panel
authenticates an API key from; a request without it falls back to session-cookie
auth.

## Create an API key in the panel

You need `apikey.read` to see the page and `apikey.write` to create a key
(`admin.read` covers reading, `admin.write` covers both). Non-admins see and
manage only their own keys.

1. Sign in and open **Admin → Access Control → API Keys**.
2. Select **Create API Key**.
3. Fill in the dialog:
   - **Name \*** — a descriptive label, for example `Billing System Integration`.
   - **Permissions** — leave **All my permissions** on to inherit everything
     your account can do, or switch it off and tick individual scopes. You
     cannot grant a scope you do not hold yourself.
   - **Expiration** — `90 days (recommended)` by default; also `7 days`,
     `30 days`, `180 days`, `1 year`, or `Never expires`.
   - **Rate Limit** — requests per minute for this key. The default is `100`;
     see [rate limits](/api/rate-limits/).
4. Select **Create API key**.
5. Copy the key from **Your API Key** into a secret manager. It is shown
   **once** — later you can only revoke and recreate it.

Every key starts with `catalyst_`:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CATALYST_API_KEY" \
  https://panel.example.com/api/servers
```

## Manage keys in the panel

- The list shows each key's status (active, disabled, expired), permissions,
  rate limit, request count, and last use.
- **Edit key** changes the name, the enabled state, and the rate limit.
  Permissions and expiry are fixed at creation — revoke the key and create a
  new one to change them.
- **Revoke key** deletes the key immediately; requests using it fail with
  `401`. Revoking an agent (node) key disconnects that node's agent, so the
  panel asks you to confirm by typing the node ID first.

## Expiry and live permission checks

- An expired or disabled key is rejected with `401` before the request reaches
  the route.
- A key never outlives its owner's permissions. On every request the panel
  re-resolves the owner's current role permissions and rejects a key whose
  scopes are no longer held (`403`). A key created with **All my permissions**
  tracks the owner's current permissions, so a demoted owner shrinks (or zeroes)
  the key automatically.

## Automate key management

The panel's own endpoints work from a script. Mutating calls need
`apikey.write`; the list and usage reads need `apikey.read`.

```bash
BASE=https://panel.example.com
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $CATALYST_API_KEY"

# Create a key. expiresIn is seconds (3600–31536000); omit it for no expiry.
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"billing-sync","permissions":["server.read","backup.read"],
       "expiresIn":7776000,"rateLimitMax":100,"rateLimitTimeWindow":60000}' \
  "$BASE/api/admin/api-keys"

# The response data.key is the full secret — store it now, it is never returned again.

# List keys, inspect usage, then revoke.
curl -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/admin/api-keys"
curl -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/admin/api-keys/<keyId>/usage"
curl -X DELETE -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/admin/api-keys/<keyId>"
```

Create the replacement key first, deploy it, then delete the old one — never
delete-then-create.

## Node credentials

Nodes authenticate with their own node ID + agent API key over the agent channel
(`/ws?nodeId=<id>`), managed through
[registering a node](/admin/nodes/registering/). Node credentials are never
valid for the user-facing API, and user API keys are never valid for the agent
channel.

## Related

[Authorization & permissions](/api/authorization/) · [Errors](/api/errors/)

# Authorization & Permissions

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/authorization/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## The model

- **Users** get powers through [roles](/admin/roles/). A request is allowed when
  the caller's effective permission set satisfies the permission the route
  requires. Roles may also carry server-scoped and node-scoped grants, merged in
  for the specific server being touched.
- **API keys** carry their own scopes, chosen at creation, and can never exceed
  their owner's permissions — see
  [Expiry and live permission checks](/api/authentication/#expiry-and-live-permission-checks).
- **Subusers** are granted a subset of the server-scoped list by the server
  owner.

## Admin bits

| Value | Grants |
| --- | --- |
| `*` | Everything (Super Admin). |
| `admin.write` | Every concrete permission, read or write. |
| `admin.read` | Every read permission: anything ending in `.read`, plus `node.view_stats`, `backup.download`, and `diagnostics.download`. |

A resource-scoped admin bit (`admin.read:<id>`) does **not** widen to all
resources.

## Permission catalog

These are the exact strings the API key and role editors offer. Fetch them live
from `GET /api/admin/api-keys/permissions-catalog`.

| Category | Permissions |
| --- | --- |
| Administration | `*`, `admin.read`, `admin.write` |
| Servers | `server.read`, `server.create`, `server.start`, `server.stop`, `server.delete`, `server.suspend`, `server.transfer`, `server.schedule`, `server.update`, `server.install`, `server.reinstall`, `server.rebuild`, `server.clone`, `server.kill`, `server.network`, `server.storage`, `server.archive`, `server.migrate` |
| Nodes | `node.read`, `node.create`, `node.update`, `node.delete`, `node.view_stats`, `node.manage_allocation`, `node.assign`, `node.server_manage`, `node.agent_control` |
| Locations | `location.read`, `location.create`, `location.update`, `location.delete` |
| Templates | `template.read`, `template.create`, `template.update`, `template.delete` |
| Users | `user.read`, `user.create`, `user.update`, `user.delete`, `user.ban`, `user.unban`, `user.set_roles` |
| Roles | `role.read`, `role.create`, `role.update`, `role.delete` |
| Backups | `backup.read`, `backup.create`, `backup.delete`, `backup.restore`, `backup.download`, `backup.pin` |
| Files | `file.read`, `file.write` |
| Console | `console.read`, `console.write` |
| Databases | `database.read`, `database.create`, `database.delete`, `database.rotate` |
| Alerts | `alert.read`, `alert.create`, `alert.update`, `alert.delete` |
| API Keys | `apikey.manage`, `apikey.read`, `apikey.write` |
| Server Content | `mods.manage`, `plugins.manage` |
| Panel Operations | `migration.manage`, `update.trigger`, `diagnostics.download` |

`GET /api/roles/permissions-catalog` appends a **Plugins** category for tokens
that enabled plugins declare in their manifest's `userPermissions`; those tokens
only exist while the plugin is installed and enabled. The API-key catalog
returns only the built-in categories above.

### Server-scoped permissions

The grantable set for one server — subuser grants and the role wizard's
scoped-access step — is `GET /api/permissions/server`:

`server.read`, `server.start`, `server.stop`, `server.kill`, `server.install`,
`server.reinstall`, `server.rebuild`, `server.update`, `server.network`,
`server.storage`, `server.archive`, `server.migrate`, `server.transfer`,
`server.delete`, `server.schedule`, `server.clone`, `console.read`,
`console.write`, `file.read`, `file.write`, `backup.read`, `backup.create`,
`backup.restore`, `backup.delete`, `backup.download`, `backup.pin`,
`database.read`, `database.create`, `database.rotate`, `database.delete`,
`alert.read`, `alert.create`, `alert.update`, `alert.delete`, `mods.manage`,
`plugins.manage`.

Server owners and full admins implicitly hold the whole set for their servers.

## When you get a 403

`PERMISSION_DENIED` means authentication worked but the identity lacks the
permission — not that the endpoint is wrong:

1. Check which identity you sent (session user vs. which API key).
2. Compare its permissions against the endpoint's requirement in the
   [API reference](/api/reference/).
3. Ask an administrator to widen the role or scope, or use a better-scoped key.
   A key is also rejected when its owner no longer holds a scope the key was
   granted.

Request the smallest scope that works today and widen later. Permission names
are stable identifiers: cache the catalog, but re-fetch it after a panel upgrade
if you start seeing unknown permissions.

## Related

- [Errors](/api/errors/) — the full code contract
- [Roles & permissions](/admin/roles/) — the operator view

# Errors

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/errors/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## Shape

Coded error responses carry a stable machine-readable `code`, a human-readable
English `error` message, and optional extras:

```json
{
  "error": "Insufficient memory. Available: 4096, Required: 8192MB",
  "code": "INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES",
  "params": { "available": 4096, "required": 8192 }
}
```

- `params` — values the panel interpolates into the localized message. Treat
  them as display data, not as a stable schema.
- `details` — an array of `{ field, message, code?, params? }` entries
  describing each rejected field, sent on validation failures.
- `requestId` — present on errors the panel's global error handler produces
  (uncaught failures, mapped database errors); quote it in bug reports.

**Branch on `code`, never on the message.** Messages are localized and may
change; codes are versioned identifiers — renaming one is a breaking change.

**Note**
Not every response carries a `code`. Body, query, and route-parameter validation
failures return `400 { "error": "Invalid request body", "details": [...] }` (the
wording varies by validator), an invalid API key returns
`401 { "error": "Invalid API key" }`, and an unmatched route returns
`404 { "error": "Not Found" }`. Check for `code`, but do not assume it is always
present.

## Codes you will meet

| Code | HTTP | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VALIDATION_ERROR` | 400 | Request shape or values rejected. Read `details` for fields. |
| `INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES` | 400 | Node lacks memory/CPU/disk/allocations for the request. |
| `UNAUTHORIZED`, `AUTH_REQUIRED`, `AUTH_EXPIRED` | 401 | No valid session or API key. |
| `PERMISSION_DENIED` | 403 | Authenticated but not allowed ([authorization](/api/authorization/)). |
| `ACCOUNT_BANNED`, `ACCOUNT_LOCKED` | 403 | The key's or session's account is banned or temporarily locked. |
| `NOT_FOUND` | 404 | No such resource (or hidden from this identity). |
| `CONFLICT` | 409 | State conflict — duplicate name, already exists, busy. |
| `SERVER_SUSPENDED` | 423 | The server is suspended; the body adds `suspendedAt` and `suspensionReason`. A few routes return it as 403. |
| `RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | Slow down ([rate limits](/api/rate-limits/)). |
| `INTERNAL_ERROR` | 500 | Panel-side failure. Retry with backoff, then report. |
| `NODE_OFFLINE`, `AGENT_COMMAND_FAILED`, `AGENT_TIMEOUT`, `NODE_AGENT_UNREACHABLE` | 503/504 | The node's agent could not be reached or did not answer in time. |
| `FRAMEWORK_*`, `IMPORT_FETCH_FAILED` | 502 | An upstream fetch (framework download, template import) failed. |

The registry lives in `catalyst-backend/src/lib/error-codes/` (common, auth,
servers, infrastructure, admin); domain codes extend the common set. The
[API reference](/api/reference/) lists per-endpoint error codes, and the panel
translates the same codes through its `errors` namespace. A few driver-fallback
codes come only from the generic mapper in `catalyst-backend/src/lib/http-error.ts`:
`BAD_REQUEST`, `DATABASE_ERROR`, `FOREIGN_KEY`, `CONSTRAINT_FAILED`,
`INVALID_RELATION`.

## Handling guidance

1. **Retry** on 429 (after `retry-after`), 502/503/504, and network failures —
   with exponential backoff and a cap.
2. **Do not blindly retry** 400/403/404/409/423 — the request itself must change.
3. **Surface the code to your users** alongside your own message; it is what
   support will ask for.
4. **Log request ID, endpoint, code, and timestamp** on every failure.

## Related

- [Authorization & permissions](/api/authorization/) — why a request gets a `403`
- [Rate limits](/api/rate-limits/) — handling `429`

# Pagination

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/pagination/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## Pagination is per-endpoint, not universal

Catalyst does **not** use one pagination scheme everywhere. Check the endpoint in
the [API reference](/api/reference/) before writing generic page-walking code.

### `page` + `limit` with a `pagination` block

`GET /api/admin/users`, `GET /api/admin/servers`, `GET /api/alerts`, and
`GET /api/nodes/:id/allocations` always return a `pagination` object:

```json
{
  "servers": [ ... ],
  "pagination": { "page": 1, "limit": 20, "total": 84, "totalPages": 5 }
}
```

| Endpoint | `page` default | `limit` default | `limit` cap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/admin/users` | 1 | 20 | 100 |
| `GET /api/admin/servers` | 1 | 20 | 100 |
| `GET /api/alerts` | 1 | 50 | 100 |
| `GET /api/nodes/:id/allocations` | 1 | 50 | 100 |

These also accept filters such as `search` (`/api/admin/users`,
`/api/admin/servers`), `status`, and `owner` (`/api/admin/servers`).

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CATALYST_API_KEY" \
  "https://panel.example.com/api/admin/servers?page=2&limit=50&search=survival"
```

Endpoints built on the shared pagination helper — `GET /api/servers/:id/tasks`,
`GET /api/alerts/:id/deliveries`, and `GET /api/nodes/:id` (its server list) —
add the same `pagination` block **only when you pass `page` or `limit`**; without
them they return the whole collection. `page` defaults to 1 and `limit` to 50,
capped at 100.

### `page` + `limit` with flat counts

`GET /api/servers/:serverId/backups` returns `backups` plus flat `total`, `page`,
`pageSize`, and `totalPages` fields. `page` defaults to 1, `limit` to 50, capped
at 100.

### `limit` + `offset` returning `{ success, data }`

`GET /api/servers` uses an offset cursor instead of pages:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CATALYST_API_KEY" \
  "https://panel.example.com/api/servers?limit=50&offset=100"
```

```json
{ "success": true, "data": [ ... ] }
```

`limit` defaults to 50 (max 500); `offset` defaults to 0. `GET /api/templates`
accepts the same `limit`/`offset` (max 100) and returns **all** templates when
`limit` is omitted.

### Full lists

Some collections are returned whole and ignore pagination parameters: nodes,
locations, nests, roles, and server allocations. Do not assume `total` or
`pagination` is present on those responses.

## Rules

- **Cap your `limit`.** Ask for what you will display (20–100). Full exports
  belong in bulk endpoints or repeated pages, not `limit=100000`.
- **Paginate to exhaustion** (`page++` until a short or empty page, or advance
  `offset` by the rows returned) rather than trusting a total — totals shift
  while you read, so reconcile sync jobs instead of assuming a stable window.
- **Cache sparingly.** Lists change constantly (server states, node health).
  Cache seconds, not hours, or re-fetch on user action.

## Related

- [API reference](/api/reference/) — the parameters each endpoint accepts
- [Rate limits](/api/rate-limits/) — page walking and request budgets

---

# Rate Limits

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/rate-limits/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## The limits

The panel applies a **global limit of 1,200 requests per minute**, bucketed per
client rather than per IP: the bucket key combines the connection, the API key
(hashed), or the authenticated user ID. Two integrations behind one NAT gateway
do not share a budget.

Each API key also has its **own request budget**, set when the key is created:

| Setting | Default | Allowed range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rate limit | 100 requests | 1–10000 |
| Time window | 60 s | 1 s–3600 s (1000–3600000 ms) |

Change it later with **Edit key** in **Admin → Access Control → API Keys**. When
a key exhausts its budget, requests made with it fail authentication with `401`
until the window refills.

Some routes are exempt from the global bucket, and some override it:

- **SSE streams** (`/api/servers/:id/console/stream`, `/events`,
  `/metrics/stream`, `/api/admin/events`, `/api/nodes/:id/agent/logs/stream`)
  set `rateLimit: false` — they are long-lived connections, not polled requests.
- **Agent-internal endpoints** (`/api/internal/*`, `/api/agent/*`, `/ws`,
  `/api/sftp/*`, file-tunnel traffic) bypass the limiter when the request carries
  valid node credentials. The same paths without them are limited like any other
  request (`/ws` allows 10,000 per minute).
- **Route-level overrides** replace the global limit for that route:
  `POST /api/auth/login` allows 30 requests per 15 minutes and
  `POST /api/auth/register` 20 per 15 minutes; the rest of `/api/auth/*` uses the
  operator-configured limit (default 60 per minute); the backup routes allow 30
  per minute.

**Note**
Counters are shared across workers and hosts only when Redis is configured.
Without it, each backend process enforces its own budget, so the effective limit
multiplies by the number of workers.

## Response headers

| Header | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `x-ratelimit-limit` | Maximum requests in the window. |
| `x-ratelimit-remaining` | Requests left in the current window. |
| `x-ratelimit-reset` | Seconds until the window resets. |
| `retry-after` | Seconds to wait, present on a `429`. |

A `429` carries code `RATE_LIMITED`.

## Stay friendly

- **Poll rarely.** Dashboards refreshing every second per server will eat the
  budget. Prefer 10–30 s intervals, and use
  [event streams](/api/websockets/) for live data instead of polling.
- **Back off on 429.** Honor `retry-after` and the `x-ratelimit-*` headers, then
  retry with exponential backoff.
- **Batch and cache.** Fetch lists once and derive views client-side; cache
  slow-moving data (templates, nests, the permission catalog).

## If you are limited during normal use

1. Reduce poll frequency and parallel fan-out first.
2. Move live views to event streams.
3. Raise the key's own rate limit, or **Auth requests** under
   **Admin → Security** — the 1,200/min global limit is fixed, not a setting.

## Related

- [Authentication](/api/authentication/) — where a key's rate budget is set
- [Errors](/api/errors/) — the `RATE_LIMITED` code
- [Realtime events](/api/websockets/) — streams that are not on the global bucket

---

# Realtime Events

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/websockets/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Polling the REST API for live state is wasteful. For anything realtime — console
output, power transitions, metric ticks — subscribe to a stream.

Browser-facing realtime is **Server-Sent Events (SSE)**. The panel's WebSocket
gateway at `/ws` carries the node-agent control plane and plugin clients, not the
console or metrics views.

## Channels

| Channel | Transport | Endpoint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Console output | SSE | `GET /api/servers/:serverId/console/stream` |
| Console input | REST | `POST /api/servers/:serverId/console/command` |
| Server events (state, backups, tasks, alerts) | SSE | `GET /api/servers/:serverId/events` |
| All your servers | SSE | `GET /api/servers/all-servers/events` |
| Server metrics | SSE | `GET /api/servers/:serverId/metrics/stream` |
| Admin entity events | SSE | `GET /api/admin/events` |
| Node agents and plugins | WebSocket | `GET /ws` |

Every stream sends a `: heartbeat` comment and a named `ping` event
(`{ "t": <epoch ms> }`) every 25 s, so proxies keep the connection open and your
client can detect a half-open one.

## Authentication

- **Console stream, console command, and metrics stream** accept a session
  cookie or an API key (`Authorization: Bearer`) — the same auth as REST. The
  console requires `console.read` and the metrics stream `server.read` on that
  server; the owner, a subuser with the permission, and admins all qualify. An
  API key must also hold the permission itself, not just its owner.
- **Server events** (`/events`, `/all-servers/events`) and **admin events**
  require a **session cookie**; an API key is not accepted there.
- **Admin events** additionally requires `admin.read`.

Unauthenticated or unauthorized subscribers get an HTTP status before any data
flows (`401`, `403`, `404`, or `503` below).

## Access limits

Long-lived streams are capped per backend process. Over the cap the connection is
refused with `503`:

| Code | Cap |
| --- | --- |
| `CONSOLE_VIEWER_LIMIT_REACHED` | 50 concurrent console viewers per server |
| `SSE_SUBSCRIBER_LIMIT_REACHED` | 100 concurrent event subscribers per server |
| `SSE_SUBSCRIBER_LIMIT_REACHED` | 200 concurrent subscribers on `/api/servers/all-servers/events`, which shares its registry with the metrics streams |
| `SSE_SUBSCRIBER_LIMIT_REACHED` | 150 concurrent subscribers on `/api/admin/events` |

## Console events

| Event | Payload |
| --- | --- |
| `connected` | `{ serverId, timestamp }` |
| `console_output` | `{ serverId, stream, data, timestamp, logId }` — `stream` is `stdout`/`stderr`; `logId` is the persisted log row id |
| `eula_required` | `{ serverId, serverUuid, eulaText, timestamp }` |
| `ping` | `{ t }` — epoch milliseconds |
| `error` | `{ serverId?, error }` |

The metrics stream sends `connected`, then a `resource_stats` event on every
agent tick (plus one immediately on subscribe).

## Server and admin events

The SSE **event name** (what `addEventListener` receives) is the type
discriminator; most payloads also carry a `type` field. Switch on the event name
and ignore unknown names — new event types are added over time and must not break
your client.

Server event names:

- `server_state_update` — power/state transitions
- `resource_stats` — CPU, memory, disk, network tick
- `backup_started`, `backup_complete`, `backup_restore_started`,
  `backup_restore_complete`, `backup_restore_failed`, `backup_delete_started`,
  `backup_delete_complete`, `backup_updated`, `backup_deleted`
- `task_progress`, `task_complete`, `task_created`, `task_updated`, `task_deleted`
- `server_operation_progress` — dense install/transfer/clone progress
- `server_files_changed`, `storage_resize_complete`, `eula_required`, `alert`
- `server_created`, `server_updated`, `server_deleted`, `server_suspended`,
  `server_unsuspended`, `clone_failed`
- `database_created`, `database_deleted`, `database_password_rotated`
- `mod_install_complete`, `mod_uninstall_complete`, `mod_update_complete` and the
  matching `plugin_*` events
- `permissions_updated` — the caller's permission set changed
- `resync` — the panel lost events (bus reconnect); re-fetch authoritative state

The admin stream (`/api/admin/events`) carries entity-level create/update/delete
events (`user_*`, `node_*`, `template_*`, `alert_*`, `role_*`, `api_key_*`,
`location_*`, `nest_*`, `task_*`, `database_*`, `network_*`, `allocation_*`,
`agent_update_*`, `node_metrics_updated`, `audit_log_created`,
`auth_lockout_created`/`auth_lockout_cleared`, `panel_update_*`, …).

## Client rules

1. **Let EventSource reconnect.** There is no server-side resume cursor: treat
   every reconnect as fresh and re-fetch authoritative state over REST.
2. **Handle the HTTP failures** (`401`, `403`, `503`) instead of
   reconnect-spinning; a refused stream will not recover without a change on your
   side.
3. **One connection per view**, then fan out locally. The panel's own SSE hub
   already shares one `EventSource` per URL across all widgets.
4. Fall back to REST polling only when streams are unavailable, and say so in
   your UI.

## Example (console)

```js
const src = new EventSource(
  `/api/servers/${serverId}/console/stream`,
  { withCredentials: true },
);
src.addEventListener('console_output', ({ data }) => {
  appendOutput(JSON.parse(data).data);
});
src.addEventListener('eula_required', ({ data }) => {
  showEula(JSON.parse(data).eulaText);
});
src.addEventListener('error', handleStreamError);

// Sending input is a normal POST, not a socket frame:
await fetch(`/api/servers/${serverId}/console/command`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
  body: JSON.stringify({ command: 'say Hello' }),
});
```

The command body is `{ "command": "..." }` (1–4096 characters) and requires
`console.write`.

## The WebSocket gateway

`GET /ws` is the bidirectional channel:

- **Nodes** connect as `/ws?nodeId=<id>` and authenticate with the node's agent
  API key in the `node_handshake` message; a socket that has not authenticated
  within 10 s is closed.
- **Plugin/browser clients** connect to the same path and authenticate with the
  session cookie on the upgrade, or with a `client_handshake` message carrying a
  session token within the first 3 s. Plugin traffic is addressed by message type
  `plugin:{pluginName}:{eventType}` with a `data` payload.

## Related

- [API reference](/api/reference/) — the REST endpoints the streams pair with
- [Rate limits](/api/rate-limits/) — why SSE streams bypass the global bucket
- [Errors](/api/errors/) — `401`, `403`, and `503` handling

---

# API Guides

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/guides/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

Copy-pasteable patterns for the jobs integrations do most. Adapt the host, key,
and IDs. Full field details live in the [API reference](/api/reference/).

## Prerequisites

- An [API key](/api/authentication/) created in the panel
  (**Admin → Access Control → API Keys → Create API Key**).
- The permissions each workflow needs — for example `server.create` to provision
  a server and `backup.read` to list backups.

## Provision a server for a new customer

```bash
BASE=https://panel.example.com
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $CATALYST_API_KEY"

# 1. Pick a template and a node (the full template list is returned by default).
curl -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/templates" | head -c 600
curl -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/nodes" | head -c 600

# 2. Create the server. Required: name, templateId, nodeId, locationId,
#    primaryPort, allocatedMemoryMb, allocatedCpuCores, allocatedDiskMb.
#    environment is a string map. Returns 201 with data.id.
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"customer-1","templateId":"<id>","nodeId":"<id>","locationId":"<id>","allocatedMemoryMb":2048,"allocatedCpuCores":2,"allocatedDiskMb":10240,"primaryPort":25565,"environment":{}}' \
  "$BASE/api/servers"

# 3. Start it, then follow the console over SSE (see /api/websockets/).
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/servers/<serverId>/start"
```

`allocatedMemoryMb` has a minimum of 512 and `allocatedDiskMb` a minimum of 1024.
The template may require environment variables — the create call returns
`SERVER_MISSING_TEMPLATE_VARIABLES` if one is absent. Power actions are
individual endpoints, not one action field: `POST /api/servers/<serverId>/stop`,
`/restart`, `/kill`.

## Nightly backup check

```bash
# List recent backups; alert if the newest successful one is too old.
curl -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/servers/<serverId>/backups?limit=5"
```

`limit` defaults to 50 and is capped at 100; the response carries `total`,
`page`, `pageSize`, and `totalPages`. Backup routes allow 30 requests per minute
([rate limits](/api/rate-limits/)).

## Rotate a leaked API key

```bash
# Create the replacement first, deploy it, then delete the old key —
# never delete-then-create (that is an outage).
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"billing-sync-v2","permissions":["server.read","backup.read"],"expiresIn":7776000}' \
  "$BASE/api/admin/api-keys"
curl -X DELETE -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/admin/api-keys/<oldId>"
```

The response `data.key` is the full secret and is returned only at creation.

## React to crashes in realtime

Subscribe to [server events](/api/websockets/) and trigger on
`server_state_update` when a server leaves `running`, then confirm via REST
before paging anyone — flapping nodes produce duplicate events during
reconnects.

## Related

- [Authentication](/api/authentication/) — create and scope an API key
- [Authorization & permissions](/api/authorization/) — the permission each call needs
- [API reference](/api/reference/) — full field and error details

---

# Plugin Development

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/plugins/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

A **plugin** extends the panel itself: extra API routes, admin and server tabs,
scheduled work, WebSocket messages, and plugin-owned storage. It is not the
same thing as a game-server mod. Server owners install those from
[Mods & Plugins](/users/mods-plugins/); this guide is for people who write
code that runs inside the panel.

If you only need to call Catalyst from outside, use the [REST API](/api/overview/)
instead.

## What a plugin can do

| Capability | Where it shows up |
| --- | --- |
| HTTP routes | `/api/plugins/<name>/…`, same session and [API key](/api/authentication/) auth as the rest of the panel |
| Admin and server tabs | Sidebar and server detail pages |
| Standalone pages | A path such as `/my-plugin` |
| UI slots | Dashboard, sidebar, and profile |
| Scheduled work | Re-registered every time the plugin is enabled |
| Events | Host lifecycle (`server:started`) and your own events |
| Storage | Key-value plus document collections, scoped to the plugin |
| Sign-in | "Continue with …" buttons on the login page |
| Role permissions | Your own permission ids, listed in the role editor and usable to gate your UI |
| License validation | Vendor-owned license checks and encrypted payloads |
| Plugin-to-plugin calls | Named functions another plugin can invoke |

Plugins run **in the panel process**. A thrown error in your code can take the
backend down with it. There is no worker isolation to rely on: isolation is not
implemented, so a manifest that declares `"runtime": "isolated"` is refused at
load time instead of running in-process.

## The pieces

Every plugin is one directory whose name equals the manifest `name`:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json          required manifest
  backend/index.js     optional backend entry (ESM)
  frontend/index.ts    optional UI entry
  frontend/frontend.mjs  optional self-contained UI bundle
  README.md            optional
  assets/              optional static files
```

That layout is what the official
[catalyst-plugins](https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst-plugins) repository
uses, and it is what the panel installer accepts. A package may contain only
`plugin.json`, `README.md`, `LICENSE`, `backend/`, `frontend/`, and `assets/`.
Anything else is rejected.

| File | Job |
| --- | --- |
| `plugin.json` | Identity, permissions, config fields, events. Validated before the plugin loads. See [Manifest](/api/plugins/manifest/). |
| `backend` entry | Default-exports `{ onLoad, onEnable, onDisable, onUnload }`. See [Backend](/api/plugins/backend/). |
| `frontend` entry | Default-exports a frontend plugin definition. See [Frontend](/api/plugins/frontend/). |

## Two ways to ship

**Marketplace package.** Build a `.catpkg.zip`, publish it from an index, and
admins install it from **Admin → Extensions → Marketplace**. The package stays
inert until an admin accepts the safety disclaimer and enables it. This is how
third-party plugins reach a panel. See [Packaging](/api/plugins/packaging/).

**Repository checkout.** The panel image compiles first-party plugins from the
`catalyst-plugins` repository at build time. That path shares the panel's React
copy, so React hooks work. A marketplace install that was not compiled into the
image falls back to `frontend.mjs`, which cannot use React hooks. If your UI
calls `useState` or `useEffect`, ship it as a repository plugin or keep the UI
free of hooks.

## Related

1. [Create a plugin](/api/plugins/creating/) — scaffold, install, enable.
2. [Manifest](/api/plugins/manifest/) — every `plugin.json` field.
3. [Backend](/api/plugins/backend/) — routes, tasks, events, WebSocket, files.
4. [Frontend](/api/plugins/frontend/) — tabs, pages, slots.
5. [Data & permissions](/api/plugins/data/) — config, storage, what you may read.
6. [Sign-in plugins](/api/plugins/auth/) — OAuth and SSO.
7. [Plugin licensing](/api/plugins/licensing/) — vendor-owned license validation and encrypted payloads.
8. [Packaging & marketplace](/api/plugins/packaging/) — `.catpkg.zip` and indexes.
9. [API reference](/api/reference/) — the host REST API a plugin can call.

## Rules

- Nothing executes before an accepted safety disclaimer. Discovery reads
  `plugin.json` only; the backend module is imported and `onLoad` runs when an
  admin enables the plugin. A version or permission change forces a fresh
  acceptance and leaves the new code disabled until it happens.
- Declare the smallest permission set you actually use. Admins see that list
  before they enable the plugin, and every host capability is gated on it.
- Never put secrets in `plugin.json` or in source. Put them in config fields
  of type `password`, and document what the operator must set.
- Register HTTP routes in `onLoad`. Register tasks, WebSocket handlers, and
  event listeners in `onEnable`, because disable clears them.
- Gate your routes on the caller, not only on your own grant:
  `config.requiredPermissions` is enforced by the host. See
  [Backend](/api/plugins/backend/#routes).
- `request.user.userId` is the authenticated user id. Use `context.getUserId(request)`.
- `context.getConfig(key)` returns the configured **value**, not the schema object.

---

# Create a Plugin

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/plugins/creating/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 20 or newer.
- A running Catalyst panel you can sign in to as an administrator.
- A checkout of the [Catalyst](https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst) repository.
  The SDK and its CLI live in that repo (`packages/plugin-sdk`). They are not
  published to the npm registry, so `npx @catalyst/plugin-sdk-cli` and
  `npm install @catalyst/plugin-sdk` do not work against the public registry.

## 1. Scaffold

The SDK is a workspace project; the CLI is not, so build it by path. From the
Catalyst checkout root:

```bash
pnpm --filter @catalyst/plugin-sdk run build
pnpm --dir packages/plugin-sdk/cli run build
node packages/plugin-sdk/cli/dist/index.js create my-plugin --template fullstack
cd my-plugin
```

There is no `catalyst-plugin` on `PATH`: nothing in the workspace depends on
`@catalyst/plugin-sdk-cli`, so pnpm never links its binary, and
`pnpm --filter @catalyst/plugin-sdk-cli …` silently matches no project. Run the
CLI through `node <checkout>/packages/plugin-sdk/cli/dist/index.js`, or alias
that. `npx catalyst-plugin` does not work either, because the package is not on
npm.

`create` options are `--template`/`-t`, `--path`/`-p` (parent directory,
default `.`), and `--typescript`/`-ts`. The default template is
`backend-only`; `--template` is one of:

| Template | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| `fullstack` | `plugin.json`, a TypeScript backend, and a React frontend with an admin tab and a server tab. |
| `backend-only` | `plugin.json` and a TypeScript backend that registers one route. No UI. |
| `minimal` | `plugin.json` and a JavaScript entry with two lifecycle hooks. No `backend` or `frontend` key, no `package.json`, no `tsconfig.json`. |

The plugin name must match `^[a-z0-9-]+$`. The schema additionally caps it at
50 characters; the CLI itself only checks the pattern. The scaffold writes the
name into `plugin.json` and into the route and tab ids, and runs `git init` in
the new directory when git is available.

Other commands, run from the plugin directory. Substitute the absolute path to
your checkout, or `alias catalyst-plugin='node "$CATALYST_REPO/packages/plugin-sdk/cli/dist/index.js"'`:

```bash
CATALYST_REPO=/path/to/catalyst
node "$CATALYST_REPO/packages/plugin-sdk/cli/dist/index.js" build   # parse plugin.json, then npx tsc if tsconfig.json exists
node "$CATALYST_REPO/packages/plugin-sdk/cli/dist/index.js" test    # npx vitest run
node "$CATALYST_REPO/packages/plugin-sdk/cli/dist/index.js" pack    # write my-plugin-1.0.0.catpkg.zip + .sha256
node "$CATALYST_REPO/packages/plugin-sdk/cli/dist/index.js" pack --out dist
```

`build` accepts `--watch` but ignores it; use `npm run dev` (`tsc --watch`) in a
TypeScript scaffold instead. It only JSON-parses `plugin.json` and echoes
`name`/`version` — it does not run schema validation, so a manifest that would
be rejected at install time still "builds". `create` always copies the
TypeScript templates; `--typescript` does not switch them off. `pack` needs
`archiver` resolvable (it is a devDependency of `packages/plugin-sdk`, hoisted
to the workspace root).

The scaffold is a starting point, not the layout the official repository
ships. Its `backend.entry` points into `dist/`, and a marketplace zip is not
allowed to contain `dist/` — see [Packaging](/api/plugins/packaging/). Every
plugin in
[catalyst-plugins](https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst-plugins) instead
authors `backend/index.js` directly and points the manifest at that file, so
there is no compile step to forget. If you did compile TypeScript, copy the
compiled entry to `backend/index.js` and repoint `backend.entry` before you
publish.

## 2. What the scaffold looks like

`fullstack` matches the layout of
[catalyst-plugins](https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst-plugins):

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  package.json          "type": "module", build = tsc
  tsconfig.json
  src/index.ts          backend; compiled under dist/
  frontend/index.ts     UI entry
  frontend/components.tsx
```

The backend default-exports the four lifecycle hooks and registers routes in
`onLoad`:

```typescript
import { defineRoutes } from '@catalyst/plugin-sdk';

export default {
  async onLoad(context) {
    const routes = defineRoutes((router) => {
      router.get('/hello', async () => ({ success: true, message: 'Hello' }));
    });
    for (const route of routes) context.registerRoute(route);
  },
  async onEnable(context) {
    context.logger.info('enabled');
  },
  async onDisable() {},
  async onUnload() {},
};
```

`GET /hello` is served at `GET /api/plugins/my-plugin/hello`.

The frontend default-exports a plugin definition. Official plugins import
`createFrontendPlugin` from `@catalyst/plugin-sdk/frontend`:

```typescript
import { createFrontendPlugin } from '@catalyst/plugin-sdk/frontend';
import { AdminTab, ServerTab } from './components';

export default createFrontendPlugin({
  manifest: {
    name: 'my-plugin',
    version: '1.0.0',
    displayName: 'My Plugin',
    description: 'A Catalyst plugin: My Plugin',
    author: 'Catalyst Developer',
  },
  tabs: [
    { id: 'my-plugin-admin', label: 'My Plugin', component: AdminTab, location: 'admin', order: 100 },
    { id: 'my-plugin-server', label: 'My Plugin', component: ServerTab, location: 'server', order: 100 },
  ],
});
```

A server tab component receives `{ serverId: string }`.

## 3. Install it on a panel

Installing is an operator action in the panel, not a CLI step on the server. On
the target panel:

1. Open **Admin → Extensions → Marketplace**.
2. Find your plugin in the list and select **Install**.
3. Return to **Admin → Extensions → Plugins**. The plugin now shows in the list,
   disabled.

That is the whole install. The panel downloads the `.catpkg.zip`, verifies its
`sha256` against the index entry, extracts it, and validates `plugin.json`. An
index entry without a `sha256` cannot be installed. The code is on disk and
**not running** until you enable it.

For the panel to see your plugin, publish the package first:

```bash
node "$CATALYST_REPO/packages/plugin-sdk/cli/dist/index.js" pack
```

That writes `my-plugin-1.0.0.catpkg.zip` and a `.sha256` sidecar in the plugin
directory. Put both behind HTTPS and add an index entry with the digest from the
sidecar — see [Packaging](/api/plugins/packaging/). Add your index in the
marketplace's **Marketplaces** rail (or with `PLUGIN_MARKETPLACE_URLS`) if it is
not the official one.

**As a local checkout** (the path the official repository uses): drop the
directory into a checkout of `catalyst-plugins` and rebuild the panel image.
The panel compiles `frontend/index.ts` into the frontend bundle. You still
need `frontend/frontend.mjs` if the plugin should render on a panel that did
not compile it in.

## 4. Enable it

1. On **Admin → Extensions → Plugins**, select **Enable** on the plugin row.
2. The safety-consent dialog opens. Tick the acknowledgement and select
   **Accept & Enable**. It lists every permission the manifest declares. Until
   you do, the backend module is never imported and `onLoad` never runs.
3. Confirm the route:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CATALYST_API_KEY" \
  https://panel.example.com/api/plugins/my-plugin/hello
```

A disabled plugin keeps its routes registered. They answer `503` until an
admin enables it. Disabling does not unregister routes; it closes the gate
and clears tasks and WebSocket handlers.

**Caution**
Enabling runs the plugin inside the panel process. Read the permission list
before you accept it. Revoking a permission later takes effect on the next
call; it does not unload the code. Uninstall is the off switch for code you
do not trust.

## 5. Develop against the SDK

The SDK and its CLI are in the [Catalyst](https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst)
repository under `packages/plugin-sdk` and are **not** on the public npm
registry, so `npm install @catalyst/plugin-sdk` fails. A scaffold's
`package.json` declares `"@catalyst/plugin-sdk": "workspace:*"`, which only
resolves when the plugin directory is itself a workspace package of that
checkout. In practice:

- The **frontend** import works without installing anything. The panel's
  `catalyst-frontend/vite.config.ts` aliases `@catalyst/plugin-sdk/frontend`
  to `packages/plugin-sdk/src/frontend/index.ts`, and the
  [catalyst-plugins](https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst-plugins) repo
  aliases it to its vendored `sdk-frontend/` copy so bundles build without the
  panel checkout.
- The **backend** entry cannot import the SDK package at runtime. Official
  plugins do not try: `backend/index.js` calls `ctx.registerRoute` directly and
  imports only `node:*` builtins and its own sibling files. The panel stages the
  plugin directory and imports the entry as plain ESM — there is no bare-import
  resolution for the SDK. If you want the SDK helpers in a backend, bundle them
  into your entry at build time (the same rule as `frontend.mjs`).

| Import | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `@catalyst/plugin-sdk` | `defineRoutes`, `defineConfig`, `definePermissions`, `defineUserPermissions`, `createTypedCollection`, `createTypedContext` |
| `@catalyst/plugin-sdk/frontend` | `createFrontendPlugin`, `createPluginApi`, `PluginErrorBoundary` |
| `@catalyst/plugin-sdk/testing` | `createMockContext`, `createTestPlugin`, `createMockLicense` |
| `@catalyst/plugin-sdk/config` | `defineConfig`, `configField`, `createConfigSchema` |
| `@catalyst/plugin-sdk/routes` | `defineRoutes`, `PluginRouteBuilder` |
| `@catalyst/plugin-sdk/storage` | `createTypedCollection` |
| `@catalyst/plugin-sdk/context` | `createTypedContext`, `defineTypedContext` |
| `@catalyst/plugin-sdk/licensing` | Backend-only vendor licensing helpers (uses `node:crypto`) |

`fastify` and `react` are optional peer dependencies. The backend entry the
panel loads must be plain ESM JavaScript — TypeScript sources are not executed.

## Worked example

[example-plugin](https://github.com/catalystctl/catalyst-plugins/tree/main/example-plugin)
in the official repository is the short tour: routes, a scoped server read, a
whitelisted status write, a scheduled task, `server:started` / `server:stopped`,
a WebSocket ping, and key-value storage. Copy that shape, then read
[Backend](/api/plugins/backend/) for the contracts those calls rely on.

Selling a commercial plugin? See [Plugin licensing](/api/plugins/licensing/)
for vendor-owned license validation and encrypted payloads.

## Related

- [Plugin Manifest](/api/plugins/manifest/) — every `plugin.json` field
- [Plugin Backend](/api/plugins/backend/) — the contracts your routes rely on
- [Packaging & marketplace](/api/plugins/packaging/) — ship the `.catpkg.zip`
- [API reference](/api/reference/) — the host REST API your plugin calls beside

# Plugin Manifest

URL: https://docs.catalystctl.com/api/plugins/manifest/
Audience: developer
Last verified: 2026-10-20

`plugin.json` sits at the plugin root. The panel parses it with the manifest
schema in `catalyst-backend/src/plugins/validator.ts` before loading any code.
A plugin that fails validation does not load.

```json
{
  "name": "my-plugin",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "displayName": "My Plugin",
  "description": "What an admin sees in the plugin list.",
  "author": "Your Name",
  "catalystVersion": ">=1.62.0",
  "permissions": ["server.read", "my-plugin.sample"],
  "permissionDescriptions": {
    "my-plugin.sample": "Shown verbatim in the safety dialog."
  },
  "userPermissions": [
    {
      "id": "my-plugin.view",
      "label": "View the sample widget",
      "description": "Shows the widget on the dashboard."
    }
  ],
  "backend": { "entry": "backend/index.js" },
  "frontend": { "entry": "frontend/index.ts", "hasTabs": true },
  "config": {
    "greeting": { "type": "string", "default": "Hello", "description": "Shown by /hello" }
  },
  "events": {
    "my-plugin:ready": {
      "payload": { "id": "string" },
      "description": "Emitted after the first successful run."
    }
  },
  "dependencies": {},
  "storageEngine": "dedicated"
}
```

## Fields

| Field | Required | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | yes | 1–50 chars, `^[a-z0-9-]+$`. Must equal the directory name in the official repository. |
| `version` | yes | `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` only (`1.0.0`). No pre-release tags. |
| `displayName` | yes | 1–100 chars. Shown in the admin UI. |
| `description` | yes | 1–500 chars. |
| `author` | yes | 1–100 chars. |
| `catalystVersion` | yes | Comparison against the running panel: `>=1.62.0`, `>1.0.0`, `=1.62.2`, `<2.0.0`, `<=1.62.2`. A bare `1.62.0` means equal. Anything that does not match that pattern is incompatible. |
| `permissions` | no | Array of strings. Defaults to `[]`. Each token is trimmed; tokens that are not `^[a-zA-Z0-9_.*-]{1,64}$` are dropped, as are duplicates. |
| `permissionDescriptions` | no | Map of permission token → 1–200 char sentence. Every key must also appear in `permissions`, or discovery fails. |
| `userPermissions` | no | Up to 32 `{ "id", "label", "description"? }` entries. Permissions you expose to the panel's role editor (the ids your frontend uses in `requiredPermissions`). Ids match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]{1,64}$`, must be unique, and `*` is rejected. `label` is 1–64 chars, `description` 1–200. |
| `backend` | no | `{ "entry": "backend/index.js" }`. Path is resolved inside the plugin directory. |
| `frontend` | no | `{ "entry": "frontend/index.ts", "hasTabs"?: boolean, "hasComponents"?: boolean }`. The two booleans are accepted and unused; the panel only checks that `frontend` exists. |
| `dependencies` | no | Map of other plugin name → exact `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. A missing or mismatched dependency is logged as an error at discovery; the plugin still loads. |
| `config` | no | Map of field name → schema object. Keys match `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_-]{0,50}$`. |
| `events` | no | Map of event name → `{ "payload": object, "description"?: string }`. |
| `authProviders` | no | Up to 8 sign-in buttons. See [Sign-in plugins](/api/plugins/auth/). |
| `storageEngine` | no | `"legacy"` (default) or `"dedicated"`. See [Data](/api/plugins/data/). |
| `runtime` | no | `"legacy"` (default) or `"isolated"`. Isolation is not implemented: a plugin that declares `"isolated"` is refused at load time (`isolated plugin execution is unavailable`), so leave the field unset. |
| `licensing` | no | Vendor-owned licensing declaration. Presence of the block declares the phone-home and is disclosed before enable. `licenseServer` is required inside it. See [Plugin licensing](/api/plugins/licensing/). |

Unknown top-level keys are stripped by the schema. Do not hide required
settings there.

## Permissions you can declare

Built-in tokens already have reviewer copy. Add `permissionDescriptions` for
custom tokens, or to replace the built-in sentence.

| Token | What granting it allows |
| --- | --- |
| `server.read` | Read server rows through `context.db.servers`. Field list is fixed; see [Data](/api/plugins/data/). |
| `server.write` | `context.db.servers.update` may change `status` only. Reaching the update method still requires table access, so declare `server.read` too. |
| `user.read` | Read user rows through `context.db.users` (no credentials). |
| `user.write` | Declared for route intent. `context.db.users.update` whitelists **no** fields, so it cannot change a user. Role changes go through `roles.assign`. |
| `files.read` | Read files through `context.fileTunnel` (`list`, `download`, `archive-contents`). |
| `files.write` | Write files through `context.fileTunnel`. Also satisfies the read ops. |
| `console.write` | Send frames to a node agent through `context.wsGateway.sendToAgent`. |
| `admin.read` | Reviewer signal that the plugin registers admin-information routes. It opens no database tables. It does satisfy `server.read`, so it also satisfies the file-read gate. |
| `admin.write` | Reviewer signal that the plugin registers admin-mutation routes. It opens no database tables. The `hasGrant` gates (file tunnel, `sendToAgent`) accept it like `*`; the literal `routes.public` and `plugin.rpc` checks do not. |
| `plugin.rpc` | `context.callPluginApi`. Checked on every call. |
| `routes.public` | Lets `registerRoute({ config: { auth: 'public' \| 'optional' } })` skip session auth. Without it those routes are forced back to `required`. |
| `auth.sessions` | `context.auth.createSession`. |
| `auth.users` | `context.auth.findUser` and `createUser`. |
| `roles.assign` | `context.auth.listRoles`, `listUserRoles`, `assignRoles`, `removeRoles`. |
| `*` | Covers every declared token and every host capability. Treated as critical in the consent dialog. |

The file-tunnel and agent-console gates use `hasGrant` semantics: `*` and
`admin.write` satisfy any token, and `admin.read` satisfies `server.read`
(which the file-read gate also accepts). Declare the narrow token anyway — the
consent dialog renders what you declared, and an admin who revokes `admin.write`
or `*` takes the whole capability away.

Custom tokens (for example `my-plugin.sample`) are stored and shown to admins.
They do not unlock host APIs. Gate your own routes with
`context.requirePermission('my-plugin.sample')`.

The SDK helper that produces the two manifest fields:

```typescript
import { definePermissions } from '@catalyst/plugin-sdk';

const declared = definePermissions(
  'server.read',
  { token: 'my-plugin.sample', description: 'Read the sample records this plugin stores.' },
);
// declared.permissions, declared.permissionDescriptions
```

Descriptions are cut at 200 characters.

## Permissions for panel users

`permissions` is the plugin's own capability list: the admin grants those
tokens to the plugin, and the host enforces them on host APIs. `userPermissions`
is the other direction — permissions the plugin invents for *panel users*, so
an admin can grant them to a role and the plugin can gate its own UI:

```json
{
  "userPermissions": [
    {
      "id": "my-plugin.view",
      "label": "View the sample widget",
      "description": "Shows the widget on the dashboard."
    }
  ]
}
```

The panel lists them under **Plugins** in the role editor (they appear only
while the plugin is enabled). Use the same ids in the frontend's
`requiredPermissions` to gate a tab, page or slot component — see
[Plugin Frontend](/api/plugins/frontend/). An id that is also a built-in
permission is ignored in the role editor: use the built-in token directly.

```typescript
import { defineUserPermissions } from '@catalyst/plugin-sdk';

export const exposedPermissions = defineUserPermissions(
  { id: 'my-plugin.view', label: 'View the sample widget' },
);
// → { userPermissions: [{ id: 'my-plugin.view', label: 'View the sample widget' }] }
```

## Config field types

The admin plugin page renders a control from each entry in `config`.

| `type` | Control | Useful keys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `string` | Single-line text | `default`, `description` |
| `password` | Masked text | `default`, `description` |
| `text` | Multiline text | `default`, `description` |
| `number` | Number | `default`, `description` |
| `boolean` | Toggle | `default`, `description` |
| `select` | Dropdown | `default`, `options`, `description` |

`config` itself is not restricted by the manifest schema, and the SDK's
`ConfigFieldDef` also accepts `object` and `array`. The admin page has no
control for those: any other `type` falls back to a single-line text field.

`enum`, `min`, `max`, and `required` are accepted by the SDK's
`createConfigSchema`, which builds a zod schema for your own tests. The panel
ignores them: the settings form saves whatever it is given, so the plugin must
validate the values it reads.

`options` may be a list of strings (the ticketing plugin does this) or
`[{ "label": "High", "value": "high" }]`. `getConfig` returns the stored value,
falling back to `default`. It does not return this schema object.

```typescript
import { defineConfig, configField } from '@catalyst/plugin-sdk/config';

const config = defineConfig({
  greeting: configField({ type: 'string', default: 'Hello', description: 'Greeting' }),
  enabled: configField({ type: 'boolean', default: true }),
  priority: configField({
    type: 'select',
    default: 'medium',
    options: [
      { label: 'High', value: 'high' },
      { label: 'Medium', value: 'medium' },
    ],
  }),
});
```

`defineConfig` returns the object you put in `plugin.json`. It does not write
the file for you.

## Events block

`events` documents payloads your plugin emits. `emitTyped` warns when a payload
is missing a field declared in `payload`, and when the event is not declared at
all; it does not type-check values and does not reject the emit. Listeners use
`context.on` — see [Backend](/api/plugins/backend/).

## Dependencies

```json
"dependencies": { "ticketing-plugin": "3.0.0" }
```

The value must be an exact `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` version — unlike
`catalystVersion`, operators such as `>=` are rejected by the schema. The
panel loads dependencies first. A missing or mismatched dependency, and a
dependency cycle, are logged as errors at discovery; the plugin still loads,
so do not rely on either to gate it.

## Related

- [Plugin Data & Permissions](/api/plugins/data/) — how `permissions` gate host APIs
- [Plugin Frontend](/api/plugins/frontend/) — using `userPermissions` ids in `requiredPermissions`
- [API reference](/api/reference/) — the panel REST API the manifest enables
